speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, April 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet (for Mr. Gray) that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

Mr. Speaker, when I left off speaking yesterday I was stating that the Government does not really care to consult Canadians on how their dollars are spent. The Liberal economic record is something that any intelligent leadership contender would want to distance himself from. Unfortunately, all of them are somewhat tarred with that brush. The new would-be leaders will not even stage an honest to goodness debate with each other as we did in our leadership race. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because they are afraid to say something that might give Canadians some type of policy, something to look forward to. All you have to do, Sir, is pick up The Toronto Sun for this morning and take a look at Donato's cartoon. That cartoon says it all very clearly.
I suppose the only positive thing to have come out of the past 16 years is the clear lesson that Canadians have learned, namely that socialism does not work. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has provided proof of that. The phalanx of Crown corporations is central to the attempt to create a socialist state in Canada, and of that there is little doubt.
The Government, through its army of state-owned enterprises, has a hand in everything. It is active in all forms of transportation, in telecommunications, in energy, in exploration, in computers and aircraft and in the nuclear, fishing, and agricultural industries. Most of them are identical. We have "Cana-this" and "Cana-that" to the point where we "Cana-do" anything right economically and we have lost what once was a proud economic record. It would be quicker and easier, Mr. Speaker, to list all the things into which the Government has not put its hand.
Today's Crown corporations represent the most massive intervention by Government in the private sector that we have
ever seen in Canada. This network of state-owned agencies outside the control of Parliament-and I say in all seriousness outside the control of Parliament-has almost as many employees and almost as large a budget as the regular Public Service. It is disgraceful.
This parallel government has been used to carry out the centralizing policies of the Prime Minister. I thank God for his denouement from the political stage. Through the CIDC, CDC, the NEP and FIRA, power has become increasingly centralized in Ottawa, and specifically in the Prime Minister's office. These corporations have siphoned off investment and jobs from the private sector. They have intervened massively in the ecomony and they have used taxpayers' money to compete with the free enterprise businesses of this great nation. The result has been the loss of foreign investment and the concomitant loss of jobs, pushing up an already high unemployment rate. These policies have bankrupted small businesses across the country, and this is in spite of the established fact that small business is the only sector that is generating new jobs today. Statistically in the last two years only the private sector has created new jobs.
The Government has invaded the free marketplace with a vengeance and with our tax dollars. When governments use our money to interfere with our livelihoods, then something has gone awfully wrong and it certainly has in Canada.
William Simon in his book entitled A Time for Truth repeatedly warns that if you lose your economic freedom, then you lose your individual freedom. Personally I do not want to see that happen in this great country of ours. When governments waste our money in this way without accounting to us for the way it is spent, then that is doubly wrong. And that is exactly what has happened through the creation of these Crown corporations, Mr. Speaker.
In response to the Opposition's repeated demands for corrective action, what does the Government do? It brings in a Bill that will only make the situation worse. If this legislation were to pass in its present form, and we intend on this side to see that is does not, accountability would be curtailed even further and Cabinet control of a significant amount of taxpayers' money would actually increase.
Exactly what is the magnitude of the problem we are considering here, Mr. Speaker? As I have already pointed out, we do not know for sure how many Crown corporations there are. We do know that annually they account for more money than do the annual budgets of some countries, for example, Switzerland, Greece and Austria. The Auditor General was by no means exaggerating when he referred to Crown corporations as sub-governments. In the countries I have mentioned, the taxpayers have control over how their dollars are spent.

The problem is that in the case of our sub-governments we have no control.

Bill C-24 will do nothing to change this sorry state of affairs. It has not happened by accident. It has come about as a result of the deliberate socialistic policies of the Prime Minister; it has been financed by taxpayers a i the gas pumps, in the hotels, motels and restaurants; by old age pensioners, farmers and fishermen; and by small business owners. All of this has been at the expense of over 1.5 million unemployed.
The Crown corporations may be "ours", but has it been worth it? A recent poll indicated that 41 per cent of Canadians believe our national oil companies should be sold, while 34 per cent do not. One Liberal leadership aspirant is already making mouthing sounds about selling off the stations of Petro-Canada. I do not think we will see that come to pass because it is contrary to the policies of these fellows.
Has it been worth the outrageous deficit, the staggering unemployment rate and the loss of investor confidence in the country? I think the answer is obvious. I would suggest, however, that it has been worth it for certain individuals. It has been worth it for Jack Horner of CN and Ivan Head of IDRC. It has been worth it for Bud Drury of the NCC and Donald Macdonald. It has been worth it for Pierre Juneau of the CBC, Jack Austin of the CDIC, Joel Bell and Bill Hopper of Petro-Canada, as well as another host of Liberal hacks. They are blatant public hacks. They are parasites of the worst kind, feeding on Canadian taxpayers and dragging down the country to a state of not a banana republic but surely of a snowball republic. I would say that it has been good for the Liberals. There have been nothing but job-creation programs.
The grave concerns expressed by the Auditor General with regard to the lack of accountability of Crown corporations are well known and totally documented. There is no need to repeat all of them, but I would like to quote from his 1982 report because it goes to the heart of the matter before us today:
Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of government activities. The growing practice of using Crown-owned corporations to conduct a widening range of government activities has so strained the capability of the existing accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibility for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds.
That was the reason every one of us was sent here by our constituents. Unlike Hon. Members opposite, we over here will not quietly sit by while the authority of Parliament is eroded in this way.
How can we be expected to carry out our responsibilities when we will be shown under Bill C-24 only summaries of the corporate plans and operating and capital budgets, and only after the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) has had a chance to determine just how much of those will be shown to the public? Are we really expected to trust the Cabinet? Are we really expected to have confidence in legislation drafted by Ed Clark? Ed Clark gave us the disastrous National Energy Program, but what was his claim to fame? It was writing a thesis on the socialism of Tanzania. That is who is running the
National Energy Program; that is the type of people we have in Crown corporations. Where is the control over Crown corporation subsidiaries? There is none. This is the area where the greatest proliferation and mismanagement have taken place.
Why are there severe restrictions on debate of legislation to set up new Crown corporations with only 30 committee days and seven hours of debate? That is closure by statute. The Government has run itself on closure and on Orders in Council ever since it came into power.
Can we imagine a Bill which purports to give Parliament more control over Crown corporations but comes equipped with built-in closure clauses? That is legislated closure before the fact. Bill C-24 contains all that we have come to expect from the Government-increased powers for Cabinet and a gag on parliamentary debate. To Hon. Members opposite I say that this Bill is totally indefensible, no matter how many of them stand in their place, no matter how many platitudes they offer supposedly from the Auditor General. One leadership candidate is speaking out against the Bill. It would be refreshing if more of them would carry the ball as it relates to Petro-Canada alone.
This Bill will do nothing to meet the real concerns of Canadians with respect to Crown corporations. How will we address the intervention of Canada Post into the marketplace, for example? Mr. Warren appeared over national television the other day. What did he say? He said if the unions demand more money, they will increase the price. That was his answer. This is happening in all Crown corporations. The post office will continue to compete with private retailers by subsidizing the operations of Consumers Distributing. It will continue to use subsidized staff to the tune of hundreds of millions dollars a year to create unfair competition, government-controlled. There will be no recourse under the new competition Bill.
Bill C-24 will do nothing to curb the huge appetite of Crown corporations such as Canadair and de Havilland. What happens to the executives who mismanage billions of taxpayers' dollars? As we are all aware, they are given bonuses of up to $20,000 for mismanagement and ineptitude. What happened in CIDA when $25 million in taxpayers' dollars was funnelled into Haiti? They knew that fraudulent payments were being made to the people in the government there. It was a proven fact. Was anyone fired? Was one word said about it? Not a word.
We know what would have happened to those individuals in the real world. They would quickly have become part of the growing army of unemployed. Under this Government they are rewarded for ineptitude and for doing nothing. How can productivity in this country be increased in that fashion? There are unending examples of this type of fiscal ineptitude both in the Government and in the sub-government. It is fitting, is it not, that Senator Austin, who was unable to get elected, controls over half the budget of the sub-government over which the public has absolutely no control? Bill C-24 has

nothing whatsoever to do with accountability. It is the reverse. What it does is increase Cabinet control over the state-owned corporations and ask Members of Parliament to trust Cabinet to make the right decisions. When we go to the polls, the people will show the trust they have in this Government. This Government has given us no reason to trust it. A government that would attempt to mislead Canadians with a Bill of this nature obviously cares not a whit about the electorate, the money extracted from it and the purposes for which it will be used.
There has been the National Energy Program, the unilateral imposition of metric, the Canadian ownership charge at the gas pumps, the Liberal slush fund for Liberal ridings, the Department of National Revenue and on and on ad infinitum. Are we really expected to trust that Government? I am afraid not. In almost 15 years the Liberals have not been able to come up with anything better than Bill C-24. I suggest that it be defeated, as that Government will be in the next election. The new Progressive Conservative Government will show Canadians that not only can the job be done, but done without porkbarrelling and done with accountability. We will show them exactly how it can be done. I urge all Members to put Bill C-24 out of its misery, or at least ensure that it is amended to the point that it will give Canadians something they really need.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue the debate on Bill C-24, the Crown corporations legislation. I would like to draw to the attention of the House the fact that the most conspicuous examples of government mismanagement in recent years have been in the operations of Crown corporations like Canadair, de Havilland and other companies which are 100 per cent owned by the Crown as well as companies like Consolidated Computer, AECL and Devco, to name just a few.
Having been burned by some of these disasters which have stemmed from lack of control, lack of accountability and lack of lines of responsibility between the Cabinet and Parliament and between the board of directors and management of the companies concerned, the taxpayers expect the Government to make a serious effort to address this problem. They expect the Government to set in place some structures, rules and systems to help avoid a repeat of these problems which have cost the taxpayers billions of dollars and which have obviously cost the Liberal Government grave political embarrassment.
Addressing those problems should have been the objective of this Bill. It should have been the objective of the Bill if Government members had understood the problem, if they were serious about addressing the problem if they were really concerned about the loss of those billions of taxpayers' dollars and if they understood the political significance of the fact that when the average voter thinks of government mismanagement, he or she thinks of Canadair, de Havilland, Maislin and AECL. The voter thinks of Crown corporations or government investments which have gone sour.
What is shocking about the legislation that has been put in front of us today is that it simply sidesteps the problem. It ignores the fundamental problem of the lack of control and the lack of accountability which led up to this tremendous loss of taxpayers' funds. That is one major reason why taxpayers and

other voters in Canada are saying that this government must go and that it must make way for a team of people who are competent in management, who understand management problems, who understand how to deal with a lack of accountability and who understand that a lack of management control leads to a loss of money. It must make way for people who understand that managers who do not know whether their superiors are the Cabinet, a public servant, a board of directors or management end up with no one controlling them. When there is too much flexibility in the system, it leads to too much ad hockery and too little discipline, both of which combine to lead to a tremendous loss of money.
It is obvious that Government members do not understand these problems. They do not understand what good management is and what good management must try to do. They do not understand the significance of the questions we ask about Crown corporations. They simply do not understand. When we ask them why the Government did not replace the directors of Canadair who preside over a company which lost $1.5 billion in one single year, they say that we are against the development of that company in the City of Montreal and that we are against job creation in the City of Montreal.
That is simply not the point, Mr. Speaker. When we ask whether they have done a cost-benefit analysis and why they are willing to spend nearly $1 billion of taxpayers' money on a new program for de Havilland, which they say is not commercially viable, they say we are out to destroy de Havilland. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how can we destroy de Havilland? The company has had a great record of success over the past 40 or 50 years but this company has undertaken the Dash-8 program which they say in black and white will not be commercially viable period. I do not understand.
What will destroy this company is not the Opposition Parties, but a lack of attention to the problem, a lack of understanding of the problem and an inability to deal with the problem on a timely basis. That is what is hurting these companies today and that is what has led them to the position that they are in today.
I would like to give some insight into the attitudes of the Ministers of this Government. We all remember the Consolidated Computer Limited debacle that took place two or three years ago. Consolidated Computer was purchased by the Government about ten years ago. It ended up being given away, effectively, by the Government at a total loss to the taxpayer of some $124 million. The Government tried to hustle the final loss past us in December, 1981, or the end of November, 1981, at the last possible minute, through supplementary estimates. The House was given no chance to consider the problem and no chance to get an understanding of the lessons which could have been learned by the mess that we had gone through.
I listened while the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) and the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) asked questions of the Minister, the same Minister
who is putting this legislation before us today, the current President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray). I listened while the questions were being put to him and then my turn came just shortly before ten o'clock. I said: "Mr. Minister, I have one question to ask you. Who in the Department was responsible for the $124 million loss?'' I asked that question four times in different ways and the answer that I kept getting was: "Look, I do not think it is right for me as Minister to reveal the name of a public servant; that is something that must be kept within the Department". He was not going to answer that question. So, I said: "I accept that, Mr. Minister. I do not agree with you, but I accept it. Let me ask you one other question. Did you find out who was responsible"? I received a double-talk answer. I said: "No, I want a straight answer, Mr. Minister, yes or no. Did you ask who was responsible for the $124 million loss?" Again I received bafflegab. I asked the question four times and each time I got the same ring around the rosy. Then I put the answer to the committee, which was not denied by the Minister. I said: "All I can take from the way you are answering the question, Mr. Minister, is that when this came on your desk you said, 'How can we sweep this under the rug? How can we avoid parliamentary concern and parliamentary debate on this? How can we avoid publicity for a $124 million loss? What is the best way to cover up this problem?' "
That is the attitude of the Ministers of this Government. That is the attitude of the Minister who presented this legislation today. I give that insight because that is what this Bill is trying to do. It is attempting to give the Government the flexibility to sweep problems under the rug. There are no precise rules for accountability. There is a lot of ministerial discretion in this Bill and that was the answer the Parliamentary Secretary gave-that the discretion is there to avoid putting things in front of Parliament if the Minister decides that he does not want to do so. That is the weakness of this Bill. There is no requirement for a precise mandate for Crown corporations. We have a general mandate in the legislation, but no mandate is required to take into account the changing circumstances under which a company is operating.
There are increasing opportunities here to rely on that favourite tool of Liberal Governments for the past 15 years- the Order in Council. The Government tells us in this Bill that it can do things by Order in Council because there are a lot of things that it does not want to put under parliamentary scrutiny. It wants to do things quietly in the Cabinet room and then have the question come out after the fact, after we cannot do anything about it, after it is totally beyond our control to have any impact on the decision that has already been made.
Bill C-24 is not what we want, it is not what we need, but sadly it is what we should expect from this Government. Let us look at some of the things that have been presented to us as Members of Parliament in this piece of legislation. Bill C-24, first of all, does not cover nearly the extent of Crown investments as it should. It omits mixed and joint enterprises-de Havilland, Canadair and investments such as Consolidated Computer. It includes only the parent companies, so there is a

great gap in the control that we as Members of Parliament will have over vast investments by the federal Government. As I said previously, there is a lot of room for ministerial discretion. Most aspects of the Bill are covered by regulation. We have not seen the regulations. As far as I am aware the Government has no intention of informing us of the regulations before the legislation is passed.
Some aspects of the Bill look pretty good at first glance. There is a requirement for the operating budgets, the capital budgets that my colleague referred to previously. The Government also has the option to exempt individual corporations from these requirements, so that we are kept in the dark like the growing of mushrooms.
The result is that Parliament could end up with less information than it is receiving now. The operating capital budgets will only be put before Parliament if Treasury Board and the Minister allow. The Bill restricts Parliament's ability to debate special Act corporations. This, as my colleague and other Members from this side have said, is a tremendous gap in the powers that we have as Members of Parliament. My colleague referred to it as closure by legislation-30 days of committee time and seven hours of House of Commons debate for the formation of Crown corporations which could have a tremendous impact on the economy and on the operations of government. There is simply no more control given to Parliament when there are big gaps like that in the legislation.
Let us look at the position of Ministers who are supposedly responsible for the Crown corporations. They are designated as the shareholders. They are the ones who are supposed to control the operations of the company, but effectively under the terms of this Bill that is fully taken away from them by either Cabinet or by Order in Council. There is no increase in real responsibility. In fact-I will develop this thought later, Mr. Speaker-when there are so many focal points of possible responsibility, either of the Minister, of the full Cabinet, of the Public Service, the board of directors, or in management, and there is no indication within this Bill as to where the final authority resides, it means that everybody's business is nobody's business. We are left floating in a sea of ill-defined responsibilities. That is bound to result in more disasters. The Minister, as others on this side have pointed out, becomes simply a post box address. That is purely and simply the result of it. The role of the board of directors, the chief executive officers and the senior officers of Crown corporations is set not by the Minister or the board of directors but by Cabinet. That is a very major weakness.
If you think back-and I encourage you to read this, Mr. Speaker-on June 7, 1983 there was a very important report released by the Senator from the other place on the operations of Canadair. This was a text book example of how Crown corporations should not be run. It pointed out all the problems from which Canadair suffered because there was lack of responsibility and lack of understanding of where the lines of authority lay. The result has been that we got into this $1.5 billion loss.

This new legislation does nothing to remedy that situation. It learns nothing from the problems we suffered and from the tremendous loss that we, as taxpayers, have underwritten here. The quality of the people who are appointed to these boards of directors by the Liberal Government will continue to be the same. We all know the problems of the Mackaseys and the Horners, but there are also the financial contributors, the bagmen for the Party and the campaign people who are on the boards of directors of these companies. I do not have anything against campaign people or boards of directors, but I do have a very serious difference of opinion when these people are put into jobs for which they have no training and no understanding as to what corporate affairs are all about, what budgets are or what corporate planning entails.
Bill C-24 does nothing to change that situation. It does nothing to indicate to these people the importance of the job which they are being asked to do and the reasons why they should not be appointed to those positions by this Government. Bill C-24 reinforces the problem we have today and leaves us in a position where the directors of these Crown corporations are eunuchs; they are cyphers and they are simply there to collect a political pay-off. The result is there is no accountability, no check and balance at the board of directors' level of the performance of the senior officers, or the company at large. Until the Liberals demonstrate by their actions that directors have a clear role to play, that they have specific responsibilities, we must expect a continuation of the problems of the Canadairs, the de Havillands, the CCIs, the Devcos, and so on.
With respect to ministerial responsibility, Bill C-24 leaves the Minister as the shareholder by law but requires the Cabinet to approve most of the major initiatives, a responsibility which one would expect the shareholders to take, such as appointments of directors, auditors, chairmen, chief executive officers, preparation of the budgets. All this is taken away from them by this legislation and put into the hands of the Cabinet. The result will be a significant lack of accountability and that simply is not going to serve the taxpayers of our country well.
Let us now look at where some of the responsibility does lie. Bill C-24 gives authority to the Governor in Council, subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance, to approve borrowings and guarantees. The Minister of Finance is provided with the final authority for these Crown corporations. What I was looking for in this legislation was something I have been asking for in this House for about three years now, that is, overall control of borrowing, not just the direct borrowing of the Government of Canada which comes under the borrowing authority legislation, but an overall authority which covers the direct and indirect borrowing of Crown corporations plus the guarantees and the letters of comfort and things of that nature which add up to the hidden deficit. I am not talking about just the $31 billion but about the larger hidden deficit of the Government of Canada of $36 billion or $37 billion. I have asked the Minister of Finance, both the previous Minister of Finance and the current Minister of Finance, for this. I have

been told it would be looked into but to date it has been totally ignored. This is a very major gap in this legislation.
The final point I would like to cover, Mr. Speaker, is the mandate of Crown corporations. This is a problem which has developed in recent years as Crown corporations have suffered some setbacks, and I use that word in a very gentle way. There have been instances such as this with AECL and with Caner-tech, where the Crown corporations, with the full financial support of the Government of Canada, have moved into areas which are not covered by their mandate at all. The result has been very unfair competition between these Crown corporations and the private sector, which previously has been able to look at that area of business as part of its own area of responsibility.
Let me give the example of Canertech. It is doing retrofits on buildings which involves a very extensive capital expenditure. What Canertech is saying to the owners of the buildings is: "We will do this business for you. We will pay for the total capital cost of it and you pay us by the savings which you make on the heating and air conditioning as a result of the retrofit". This is a very good deal. It is a deal which no one can refuse. But it is a deal which no private sector company could possibly offer. I say in the best of parliamentary spirit to the Parliamentary Secretary, since the Minister is not here, to take back this thought of giving Crown corporations and federal Government wholly-owned companies such a mandate and give them a much clearer mandate so that they are restricted in their ability to compete on unfair terms with the private sector.
In conclusion, this Bill is a major disappointment to us as Members of Parliament. We have no confidence that the Government has learned the lessons of the past and that is an overwhelming reason not only for a change of government but to scrap this Bill and allow a new government which understands the problem to bring in better legislation which will deal effectively with the situation.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate because I believe it is a very important debate. All of us realize that Crown corporations have taken an increasingly important role in implementing the policy of this Government. As a result, any changes which are made to the way in which these Crown corporations can act, in the way they can respond and generally do their business, becomes increasingly important to deal with in this House.
First in my remarks today I would like to comment on what essentially we had hoped to see in the Bill, in fact what, I suppose, we expected to see in this particular piece of legislation. What we wanted to see dealt with was ministerial responsibility for Crown corporations, which becomes very important when we look at a simple example, one with which I am familiar, of Canada Post. Time and time again we have addressed questions regarding that particular Crown corporation in this House of Commons only to have the Minister say: "I will have to check with the responsible people in Canada Post. I will have to see what they say". The Minister never gives a direct, straight answer here in the House of Commons. It is always a circuitous answer. That is the kind of thing which we as parliamentarians want to address because we see it as being absolutely essential to make sure that Crown corporations are responsible to Parliament.
The second thing we had hoped to see in this particular piece of legislation is a statement of principle on the role of Crown corporations. What is happening with them? In what direction are they intending to move? That has to be important to any kind of parliamentary overview of Crown corporations in our present set-up.
Third, we looked for a classification system of Crown corporations which was based essentially on the level of subsidization which they received from the Government. In other words, if you have a Crown corporation which is accepting a high level of funding from Parliament, then obviously it has to be very much accountable to Parliament because it must be responsible for the use of public funds, taxpayers' money. On the other hand, if a Crown corporation receives little or no funding from Parliament, perhaps then we can be a little less stringent in relation to that corporation.
The fourth thing we saw as being significant and important to this legislation is that there should be controls over Crown corporation subsidiaries. In other words, the subsidiaries of any particular Crown corporation must be held accountable, must be responsible and must in some way answer to Parliament, thereby to Members of Parliament, and ultimately to the Canadian people.
The fifth thing we were looking for is comprehensive public business plans. The Canadian people have a right to know where any public agency is going. They have a right to know what kind of plans are being made for that agency and in which direction it intends to move.
The sixth thing we looked for is very important. It is an effective and meaningful audit by the Auditor General. That is very important when we consider the number of examples we have seen lately that have demonstrated waste by Government.
We also wanted to have some form of standardized accounting procedures. We have heard a lot of discussions on the significance of comprehensive auditing lately. We feel a need to have those accounting procedures standardized.
The eighth thing which we felt was essential was to have boards of directors comparable to those in the private sector. In other words, they must have some clout, authority, impact and ability to give direction to the organization they are dealing with.
The final thing which we were looking for is something which I personally feel is extremely important. We wanted to see a joint committee of the House of Commons and the
May 1, 1984

Senate set up with a mandate to initiate periodic reviews of Crown corporations. That becomes essential.
A short time ago I was very pleased to work with the special committee on parliamentary reform. We spent a good deal of our time studying this particular area of concern. We studied it because we felt there was a tremendous interest by Canadians in knowing what is happening with Crown corporations. Canadians felt a need to make sure that these corporations were accountable to Parliament. We spent a good deal of time considering various ways of making sure that sort of thing was addressed.
One of the recommendations which I thought was significant was put forward in the report commonly referred to as the Huntington-Lachance report. That was a recommendation to set up a special committee to look into what we called the quasi-government agencies. It would be a committee to look at Crown corporations which are once removed from Parliament, but which at the same time play a significant role in the policies of the Government and the directions that these corporations were taking. We felt that kind of scrutiny was essential.
We needed those things because of the central role of Crown corporations and other agencies and their growing impact upon Canada.
I would like to speak for a few minutes about why we were looking for those things to be done and why we expected to see them in this particular legislation. Anyone who has paid any attention to the subject for any amount of time will know that there has been a great deal of debate and interest in this subject. There have been various reports by the Auditor General calling for the nine basic points which I have discussed briefly. The Lambert Commission is another example of a group and a report which was seeking reform in the way that Crown corporations were dealt with in Parliament. There is the Privy Council Office blue book. There was previous consideration in the forefathers of this particular Bill-Bills C-27, C-123 and C-153. In addition to those Bills and reports there have been a number of academic papers done on this subject across Canada, all of which have stressed the very important need for reform in our ability to deal with Crown corporations.
In addition to that, probably one of the most important elements calling for reform has been Canadians themselves from coast to coast. Any Member of Parliament, whether on the Opposition or Government side, will tell you that Canadians are very much concerned with the impact Crown corporations are having and how they are held accountable by Parliament for the Canadian people. All of the groups which I have just referred to expected to see these nine basic principles addressed. All of them stated the need for reform and control over Crown corporations.
The reason these various groups have come up with these essential points can probably be broken down into five general statements. The first reason or need for reform is the dramatic increase in the number of Crown corporations. I understand that the piece of legislation which we are debating today will apply to 183 Crown corporations, all of which have an impact
Financial Administration Act
of varying degree upon our country and the policies and directions taken in our country.
Second, there has been a significant increase in the number of Crown corporations and agencies and in their importance, but there has not been the corresponding balance of accountability. That is the sort of thing we want to encourage.
The third reason is that there has been no comprehensive system of control or accountability. Another reason dealing with accountability is that accountability has tended to be spread out. When accountability is spread out it becomes diluted and ultimately there is no accountability.
My colleague who spoke before me addressed the fifth reason. It is the idea of political appointments of directorships. When that happens frequently it becomes increasingly important to have well-defined regulations, guidelines and policies to ensure that things are carried on in a businesslike and efficient manner.
I have essentially spoken about what I feel we need. I have spoken about who I believe has suggested the kind of things we need. I have also spoken a little bit about why I think we need these particular amendments. I would now like to touch briefly upon what I believe we have ended up with in this Bill. As I see it, it has essentially been a contrast between what we needed and what we ended up with.
I would first like to discuss ministerial responsibility. By looking at the way things are laid out we find that the Minister shares his responsibility. He shares it generally with Treasury Board and specifically with the Finance Minister. He shares it generally with Cabinet and specifically with the board of directors. There is a lot of shared responsibility. It goes back and forth and in and out. We end up with no one individual taking absolute responsibility. This can have a tendency to create confusion and misunderstanding. The essential concern is that with that watered down approach individuals will be passing the buck in an endless cycle and no one will take responsibility.
I will refer back to the Crown corporation Canada Post. There is a situation within Canada Post which is having a tremendous impact upon Canadians and is causing a great deal of concern to small business people across the country. Canada Post is doing some testing on the idea of getting into the catalogue business by way of serving as a counter to take orders. Several times in the House the Minister has been asked what is going on, what is happening, where we are going. Time and again his response has been that he will check it out. The ultimate response we have received is that Canada Post will make a decision after the results of those tests are received. The question that Parliament wants answered is: If the results of those tests are good for Canada Post, is that all that is required for it to proceed or does it have to be good for the business community at large and the Canadian public? Those are the issues which need to be addressed.
Let me give an example. There is a lady in my area who makes her living by running a shop in which she takes orders

May 1, 1984
Financial Administration Act
for a particular catalogue company. That provides her with her livelihood to support her family. As well, she has two or three part-time employees who earn part of their living from that particular business. If Canada Post proceeds to open up this type of business in the post office in that small community, that woman will immediately be out of a job. Her business will cease to exist. Her family will have lost its means of support. Is that the kind of action we as parliamentarians want to encourage? I do not think so. The only way we can prevent that from happening is by having an accountable and responsible Minister in the House who can stand up and give a definitive answer and make a decision. One would certainly doubt that this is the case at the present time.
Let me proceed and talk about the statement of principles regarding Crown corporations. I do not see a clear definition of that in this legislation, nor is there a classification system according to the subsidization level that I referred to in my third point. Rather, there seems to be a somewhat arbitrary list. For example, Air Canada is put together with CDIC. However, what is included within CDIC? It is Canadair. One corporation has been very successful while the other has not.
There is a corporation and an administrative agency lumped together. These are Canada Post and the National Capital Commission. It is difficult to understand how they relate to each other. Of course, the joint or mixed enterprises in which government agencies are involved are not even included. I think that lack of a comprehensive guidance system, which we believe is so essential, has allowed, and in fact in some ways encouraged, Crown corporations to invent their own policies and objectives. How can Crown corporations really be effective policy instruments without that kind of clear direction and guidance?
The question remains: Is this legislation going to create a standard approach to Crown corporations? Will it end the jumbled and ad hoc approach that exists at the moment and make an actual improvement? We on this side suggest that there will not be much significant improvement as a result of this particular piece of legislation.
We do not believe there is a meaningful attempt in this legislation to control the creation of Crown corporations, their subsidiaries or affiliates. We do not believe there is an assurance for the presentation of clear business plans so that there will be good, clear financial reporting. We do not believe there will be a standardizing of the necessary accounting procedures to ensure that its practices are clear and understandable to allow us quickly and efficiently to understand if the corporation is operating as we believe it is.
I believe there are a number of reasons why there is no real attempt to accomplish those goals. First, there are contradictions within the legislation. Second, this Bill has not amended the original Crown corporations and incorporation legislation that allows open-ended treatment of these particular agencies by Cabinet.
The third reason concerns the wide exemptive clauses that are imbedded in this particular Bill. The final reason involves
the regulatory powers. One only needs to look at Clause 135(4) to have an example of that. It reads:
The Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, make regulations
(a) exempting a specified Crown corporation or a Crown corporation of a specified class from the application of subsection (3)-
One can see that exemptions are already taking place. There are loopholes in the legislation that allow a particular corporation to get around the particular concerns that we believe should be addressed in the Bill.
This legislation also allows the exclusion of individual Crown corporations from the requirements of the Bill. That exclusion is contained in the clause to which I just referred. I immediately see a red flag whenever such a provision is brought to my attention. I know there are some dangers inherent in such a clause. It also provides that regulation will allow individual Crown corporations to be treated differently from others. Again, one must see a red flag warning because there is concern for potential problems and difficulties.
Therefore, in my view this Bill is one that advocates the ad hoc treatment of Crown corporations rather than the standardizing of the approach. I think this legislation goes part way in clarifying the role of the auditor. The Bill makes some clarifications in this case, but since it is a very important area it is not sufficient to move part way. Essentially, the Bill limits the scope of the special examinations by the auditor. For example, Clause 148 indicates that he cannot really get involved in reviewing policy. That is very important because we as parliamentarians want to make sure that policies are being enacted and carried out.
I thank you for the time given to me, Mr. Speaker. It is an important piece of legislation but I think it is inadequate. We are not satisfied with it and I will not be supporting it.

Mr. Speaker, I have some questions for the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) concerning the Bill. I am not sure that he has read the same Bill as I.
He talked a great deal about the question of ministerial responsibility. It seems to me that the Bill clearly sets out that there will be a Minister designated for each Crown corporation. Of course, decisions are made by Cabinet but there is only one Minister who is on the firing line, whether it is during Question Period in the House or when legislation is put through the House. Whether the Minister is defending his estimates, the corporate plan, the budget, the auditor's report or the Auditor General's report, it is the individual Minister who is responsible.
In our system of collective Cabinet responsibility, I find it difficult to understand how the Minister who is designated to be responsible for a particular Crown corporation is somehow not responsible. In the case of Crown corporations which are totally owned by the Government, he is the shareholder and there can be no question about his responsibility.

The Hon. Member raised the issue of Canada Post and its trial business with the Consumers Distributing Company. This Bill gives the responsible Minister directive powers. I am not certain this is contained in every special Crown corporation Act but clearly this Bill is one which overrides all other legislation relating to Crown corporations. All Crown corporations must comply with it. I suggest that meets the concern that the Hon. Member has already expressed. Clearly, the powers of the Bill apply to wholly-owned subsidiaries just as they apply to parent Crown corporations.
The Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) I believe mentioned one corporation in which the Government has an interest or share. I am not clear how the Government can completely control a company when it only has a partial investment. Clearly, this Bill provides that where there is 100 per cent ownership, those subsidiaries will be subject to the same directive powers as the wholly-owned parent Crown corporation.
With regard to auditing, the provisions set out in the Bill are that generally accepted accounting principles must be used. These principles are contained in a book that is approximately four inches thick and they guide and control all Canada Business Corporation Act companies. It provides that not only must those accounting principles be used, but the Minister may require that stronger provisions be made.
I agree with his argument that the House should consider whether it wants to have a special Crown corporation committee or a joint committee with the Senate, but that is a question for the House rules committee to deal with. I do not think that matter needs to be dealt with in this Bill.
Clearly with the number of corporations, I believe it is 60-some parent Crown corporations and many subsidiaries, it would be impractical not to have those corporate plans, the budgets, the audits and so on all referred to regular standing committees. It seems to me it would be impractical to have one special committee of the House deal with them on an ongoing basis.
The Hon. Member suggested that the Bill does not cover the growth of Crown corporations. Clearly it is set out in this Bill that there are only two ways Crown corporations can be established. One is through the Canada Business Corporations Act, which the Government has used in the past. When Crown corporations are set up under that provision now, a motion has to be brought in the House stating exactly their powers and prerogatives. The motion would have to be referred to a committee for some 30 sitting days and then it would be subject to at least seven hours' debate in the House as well. If it was a special Bill, such as the CDIC Bill which is before the House now, something like Petro-Canada, or other major pieces of legislation relating to Crown corporations, these special cases would continue to be brought forward under special legislation where there is no limitation on debate or discussion.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-24 with a great deal of apprehension. I see in this Bill exactly the same process that was imposed when the National Energy Program was introduced into this House of Commons.
First, Bill C-24 was an initiative by the Government for the so-called control of Crown corporations because of the pressure building across the country and because of a position which our Party took in laying down policy. We indicated some of our ideas that were necessary for Canada and the taxpayer to gain control of a government, a hidden government, and I am referring to Crown corporations.
I think we all know, Mr. Speaker, that the total number of people employed by Crown corporations exceeds the total number of people employed in the federal civil service. It is clear that these corporations have to be brought under control. The Government, at the urging of this Party, has introduced Bill C-24. The Bill is a typical smokescreen which we have seen this Government use on the taxpayers of Canada time and time again. This Government is introducing legislation and tying every major point of control in that legislation to regulations that will be imposed or set up after the Bill becomes effective; after the Bill is passed by this House. Then we will see the regulations and the regulations will be tied to the very substantive clauses within the legislation.
Let me give you an example, Mr. Speaker. The National Energy Program was introduced and the regulations were introduced afterwards. These regulations gave wide discretionary powers to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It is the Minister who can determine who will or will not get grants which are being paid for by the taxpayer for off-shore drilling. It is the Minister who by regulation will determine whether there is or is not enough Canadian content for compa-

May 1, 1984
Financial Administration Act
nies to become eligible for grants to drill in the Beaufort Sea or on Canada Lands. It is the Minister with discretionary powers, not tied to legislation but tied to regulations, which allow him to determine who in fact will get a contract and who will not. That takes the complete control, the complete accountability, out of Parliament and puts it into the Minister's hands.
Those huge regulation-making powers of the Government insulates a Crown corporation from any public scrutiny, any parliamentary scrutiny. I ask you, Sir, what individual would invest in a company and allow that company to take part in the kind of activity required of it that may be set down in its by-laws? What individual investor would allow that to happen if a company were exempted in all cases from tabling before that investor the result of its year's activities through a profit and loss statement showing how the company spent its money, the investors' money? This practice is fundamental to the business world. Individual investors would not accept exemption of the tabling of a profit and loss statement and neither should taxpayers.
Crown corporations must be accountable to the Members of the House of Commons who represent the taxpayers and shareholders of Crown corporations. What many people fail to realize but are starting to understand is that Crown corporations like the CNR, Air Canada and Petro-Canada must be held accountable to the shareholders, namely the taxpayers. They are not the Government; they are the taxpayers of the country. Crown corporations must be made accountable, and this legislation will not bring that about.
As I said, virtually every clause of substance within Bill C-24 has attached to it a regulation-making power by which government, not the people accountable to the taxpayers, defines how the clause will operate or which Crown corporations can be exempted. Without seeing the regulations, which the Government continually stonewalls and refuses to table in the House of Commons, how do we know how the Government intends to use the Bill? It is absolutely impossible to expect Members of Parliament representing the taxpayers of the country to pass Bill C-24 without knowing beforehand how the Government intends to use it.
I hearken back to the Petro-Canada Act. That company was formed so that the Government would have a window on the industry. There had been some poor forecasts of oil and gas reserves in Canada. The Liberal Government of the day brought in an Act to form Petro-Canada. Its members now say that Petro-Canada is ours. It is not ours, it is theirs, because that company is not accountable to Canadian taxpayers. The original intention was to form a window on the industry, as I said. It has grown by taking over and purchasing other companies. The clear intention of the Government has been to make it very large and unaccountable to taxpayers. That cannot continue. That was not the original intention. If in the debates at that time we had asked the Government what it intended to do, its members would have said: "We do not intend to open
up service stations across the country". By regulation they have been able to do that because the Government controls what happens to Petro-Canada.
A mirror of the Petro-Canada legislation is the Canagrex legislation. Because of the regulatory powers vested in that legislation, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) can open up corner grocery stores from coast to coast. If we ask him whether that will happen, he will say: "Of course we will not do that; we never intend to do that". There is lack of control by taxpayers, the people who indirectly own every lock, stock and barrel of those Crown corporations. We cannot go to those Crown corporations to obtain the inside information which is required by investors. It is ludicrous, absolutely ludicrous, when we as taxpayers and as Members representing taxpayers are not privy to the information within those companies concerning their day to day operations because it is a closed door.
The Auditor General of Canada cannot go to Crown corporations and demand that their books be opened to him. The chairmen and presidents of those companies have stated publicly, as all Hon. Members of the House know, that the Auditor General has no business within our Crown corporations. The Auditor General is appointed by the House of Commons to account for the spending of taxpayers' dollars. Everyone agreed that the Auditor General should be the watch-dog and should point out where money was being wasted or spent unwisely. He is not privy to information from Crown corporations unless Crown corporations on their own or the Minister decide to open the books to him. We see this fiasco time and time again.
The very sad state of affairs of Crown corporations today will not be covered or changed by this legislation. Appointments of boards of directors and chief executive officers are made and approved by the Minister or some of his colleagues. That has clearly been abused in the past and continues to be abused. I will not name specific appointments but there have been appointments of clear political hacks. The time has come for every Member of the House of Commons to be satisfied that Crown corporations have the best possible choice of people in chief executive officer positions and on their boards. We have had case after case of appointments to various boards of Crown corporations where the people appointed had absolutely no concept of how business was run or even what the Crown corporations were supposed to do.
Crown corporations are needed in a mixed economy like that of Canada's to provide service where the private sector does not have the capability to do so. We have seen it with the Northern Transportation Company, with which I am familiar. It operates off the eastern Arctic. It operated a tug and barge service from Fort McMurray up to Uranium City and all points in between. That Crown corporation decided five years ago to sell off that company, and some of the chief executive officers or members of the board were to try to buy it. They used the excuse that Uranium City was shutting down and drove the profit margin of the Fort McMurray to Uranium City part of the operation into the ground so that they could

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, has some serious flaws. The Act will not be binding. It is just more window dressing and another
Financial Administration Act
Liberal smokescreen. Bill C-29 will be coming up for debate in the near future. It contains a clause which states:
This Act is binding on an agent of Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province that is a corporation, in respect of commercial activities engaged in by the corporation in competition, whether actual or potential, with other persons, but not in respect of commercial activities engaged in by the corporation that are directly associated with its regulatory activities.
That is what is weak in Bill C-24, namely that it is not binding. When we see the disgraceful performance of our Crown corporations, Bill C-24 should be more binding. It took this Government five years to bring forward this legislation. It lacks several important features that are contained in Bill C-27. In 1979 it took the Conservative Government six months to begin the clean-up of the Crown corporation mess.
Bill C-24 does not cover mixed and joint enterprises. Although it catches 183 Crown corporations and subsidiaries, the legislation does not cover 109 Crown corporations, mixed and joint enterprises and their subsidiaries. It is strange that it would leave out 109 Crown corporations. It is impossible to know the effect of this Bill because everything is done by regulation and we have not seen the regulations. Assuming the Bill is passed, all regulations will be made by the Government behind closed doors. In the majority of instances they will not be made public. Therefore, Bill C-24 is just mere window dressing.
When the Canada Post Corporation Act was formed in 1981, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn) introduced an amendment asking that the accounts and financial transactions of the corporation be audited annually by the Auditor General. That would be a complete audit. It was voted down by the then Liberal Government.
Bill C-24 is supposed to bring more accountability to Crown corporations. Bill C-31, recently tabled by the Government, an Act to amend the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act, states:
All that portion of subsection 17(2) of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act following paragraph (b) thereof is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"shall not exceed thirty million dollars".
That is increasing the borrowing authority just like that. The current level is $20 million. The board will have the power to borrow an additional $10 million with absolutely no explanation. The manager of that corporation is a local Manitoba Liberal who is obviously going to carry on in the Liberal tradition. Their solution to all problems is to spend more borrowed money. There is no explanation or accountability clause, no calling in the corporation to explain the increased borrowing.
Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs are parading around the country. I refer to John Turner and the others who are running for the leadership of the Liberal Party. They have a goodies list, bribing taxpayers with their own money. Each one of them has the qualifications to take over as leader of the Liberal Party, especially John Turner who, when he was Finance Minister, introduced the "blank cheque government" to Canada. He played a large part in the uncontrolled spending.

I have noticed that a number of Liberal members have complained about the post office venture into Consumers Distributing and I hope that they will put some pressure on the Minister who is responsible for Canada Post so that he will take some direct action to have Canada Post withdraw from the Consumers Distributing venture.
That venture is causing serious concern across Canada. The Canadian Retail Hardware Association has expressed its concerns about a Crown corporation competing directly with that association and its operations. Mr. Thomas M. Ross, the executive director of the Canadian Retail Hardware Association, pointed out the following in a letter to me dated April 25, 1984:
It is my understanding that Mr. Warren's mandate at Canada Post is so broad, that he can really do anything he desires. If this is the case, I am greatly
troubled as to the outcome of this affair since Mr. Warren seems to have "painted himself into a corner".

The list goes on and on. All of those people have cars and we do not know how many of them have chauffeurs. However, I cannot get an answer from a Crown corporation that is supposed to be accountable to Parliament and to the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the time has come when all large hospitals and medical schools must have a formal ethics committee. With the current rapid social transformation, and with the continuing advances in medical technology and techniques, doctors and society at large face dilemmas beyond the imagination of other generations.
It is not enough, as is the custom now, for complex ethical decisions to be made at a meeting of the medical advisory board of a hospital, or by a special committee struck for a specific issue. A formal ethics committee in a hospital must consist of medical staff, social workers, religious representatives, and legal advisers. Less formal committees are more ideal in difficult situations such as making a decision as to whether or not to discontinue life support systems and should, therefore, involve only people most closely involved with the patient-the family, the doctor, and the religious adviser.
These groups in their discussions need the expertise of a person trained to deal with the ethical question, that is, an ethicist. Such people may come from a variety of professions, medicine, law, philosophy or theology. At least one year's intense training is desirable to prepare such individuals. There are only a handful of such persons at the moment in Canada. As an important matter of concern, I feel that financial support from the Government is the stimulus which is required to encourage and promote the establishment of the essential services of ethicists throughout our country.

Has the Prime Minister taken any action, or will he, to terminate this very obvious attempt, manoeuvre, to get around the Prime Minister's own very worthy guidelines?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the exchange yesterday between the Hon. Member and the Hon. Minister of Justice. I understood the Minister to say that Mr. MacDonald was not being paid by the Government, that he was a participant in a company which did contract with the Government, and that company was receiving money from the Government on contract, but that Mr. MacDonald himself was not. That is what I understood the Minister to say yesterday. I see the Hon. Member nods in assent. If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing I can see that is untoward in that.
I am sure even in the Tory leadership campaign there were active people in various companies dealing with the Government, whether it be the public utility companies, or the Bell Telephone company. I am sure some of the corporate elite supported Mr. Mulroney's campaign. The fact that the company to which they belonged was contracting with the Government did not cast any doubts on the conduct of those members. In other words, if the facts are as I understood them, and as the Hon. Member understood them, I do not see that they contravene the guidelines.

My supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, really relates, I suppose, to the spirit of the whole necessary activity of establishing conflict of interest guidelines. I merely ask the Prime Minister to put his mind to a manoeuvre that obviously circumvents the spirit of those guidelines. Unless the Prime Minister is asking for each of the leadership campaign candidates not only to reject his policies but also to reject the spirit of this own guidelines, surely the spirit is that there should be no appearance of conflict as well as no actual conflict? There are other cases, Sir. Here is a very obvious one in which that spirit is being circumvented. It is a very easy manoeuvre. Surely the Prime Minister still has enough power in his Cabinet to indicate that this sort of thing should stop. We are using taxpayers' funds to further a leadership campaign, and that should not happen.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
