Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be able to speak on this Bill today. I have had the opportunity to read Hon. Members' remarks as recorded in Hansard and to hear some comments made by Hon. Members about the Bill. I do not choose to repeat a number of those points today.
I believe it is of unusual interest to note that when we speak of Crown corporations these days, we are for the first time in our history speaking more and more of Crown corporations in general. That was not our practice in the past. Historically, Crown corporations have been brought to the attention of the public and discussed in the House primarily in specific terms. We have discussed a specific Bill or a specific matter relating to a specific Crown corporation for a specific purpose. By and large we have not for many, many years had any significant debate regarding what is to be the role, function and purpose of Crown corporations.
Throughout our history, Mr. Speaker, Canadians have been very pragmatic about what Crown corporations are supposed to do. We have not engaged in any excessive ideology about them. We have throughout time tried to organize Crown corporations to do specific jobs. These specific jobs were primarily jobs relating either to a specific social objective or very often relating to questions of economic growth. In the early part of this century in particular, we found that Crown corporations-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Could we have order in the House, please?

Thank you for doing your best, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, Crown corporations have traditionally been used for specific purposes, either for pursuing social goals or economic growth. In the early part of the century in particular, Crown corporations were primarily concerned with economic growth. That is why when we come to a debate on the role, purpose, function and accountability of Crown corporations, we are not using language which we have ever used before.
The Parliament of Canada and the Government of Canada have been able to depend upon the understanding of most Canadians that Crown corporations were established for a good and sufficient purpose-to achieve either social or economic goals. That, of course, lasted until the alarm bell was sounded by the Auditor General's report of 1976. As in Lewis Carroll's novel, Crown corporations just "growed up like Topsy". There was no coherent sense of what their purpose was in a new time, in a new age, in the 1970s.
It is worthwhile repeating the sentence that the Auditor General used in 1976 in his annual report. It is simple but devastating. He said that we now have a "weak and ineffective
May 1, 1984

control of public spending through Crown corporations". That was in 1976. His report to Parliament referred to the weak and ineffective control of public spending through Crown corporations.
Six years later he had this to say in his report of 1983:
Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of government activities. The growing practice of using Crown-owned corporations to conduct a widening range of government activities has so strained the capability of the existing accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibility for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds.
The Auditor General's report of 1983 hearkens back to his earlier report of 1976. He noted that during the six-year period, nothing was done to improve the situation. It was worthwhile for him to note, as he did in his report, just where we had been for the last 20 years in terms of the size and the value of Crown corporations.
In 1962, 22 years ago, there were 28 Crown corporations in this country which controlled $8.4 billion worth of assets. There were 28 Crown corporations; $8.4 billion worth of assets. Twenty years later, in his report of 1983, he noted that there were over 300 Crown corporations employing 263,000 people, with assets of $74 billion and liabilities of $63 billion. We had gone that far in 20 years with almost no debate on what was the purpose, function and accountability of Crown corporations.
That is why we on this side of the House have been saying to the Government for years-certainly for the six years that I have been here: "You have heard the Auditor General's report, you have read the report, you have established the Lambert Commission, and you have heard from the Standing Committee on Public Accounts". Why has nothing been done? All the boards, commissions and special purpose bodies that were established in order to deal with the problem were totally ignored by the Government.
That is why we looked forward to Bill C-24 when it came in. We were looking to see how close it would come to a similar Bill which was established by the Government of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) in 1979-80.
As other Members of the House have noted, the Bill that was brought in four years ago by the Government of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead was vastly superior to the Bill that is before us. The current Bill deals not at all with the one fundamental question that most people walking the streets of the country, if they have any interest in Crown corporations at all, simply want to know, namely: Who is responsible, who is accountable, for federal Crown corporations in Canada? It is a question that might be asked at the provincial level where there are many, many Crown corporations as well. Indeed, there are public utilities at the municipal level which carry out similar functions to that of Crown corporations.
The questions that people ask not only refer to financial management. The real question is: Who is accountable? Is it the Minister? Is it the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray)? Is it a specific Minister in the House? In Bill C-24, is the Minister made responsible? Can Canadians now say: "We
Financial Administration Act
know the Minister is responsible"? If you read the Bill, the power and responsibility of the Minister is totally stood on its head because the Minister has responsibility but no power. This Bill takes power away from the Minister and gives it to the Cabinet.
If it is not the Minister who is responsible, then maybe it is the board of directors of the corporations. That is not true either. If you read the Bill you will note that the powers which would normally be assumed by a board of directors are also sucked away and given to Cabinet. If it is not the Minister and it is not the President of the Treasury Board and it is not the board of directors, then maybe it could be Parliament. After all, when the Auditor General first of all sounded his alarm in 1976, it was Parliament he was talking about. Seven years later in his 1983 report-since his former report had been ignored by the Government-he said on page 15:
I remain concerned-
Seven years later he is still concerned because nothing has been done.
-about the Government's and Parliament's monitoring and controlling of Crown-owned corporations. During the past year, circumstances in a number of Crown-owned corporations have further illustrated the existing deficiencies. For simplicity, I describe only the events involving Canadair Limited and the Canada Development Investment Corporation ... to illustrate the continuing accountability deficiencies.
He goes on to point out that we are talking about six basic ways to control corporations. First of all is authorizing and mandate, Financing, directing, controlling, reporting and auditing. I will not go through all of those points. The questions related to reporting, directing, auditing and controlling have been dealt with by other Members.
I want to talk about the first one. The Auditor General's report makes it clear that when he talks about accountability, he talks about authority and mandating. That is the best example that we can use and that is what I would like to talk about. He indicated that the essence of accountability, in the first instance, finds itself not in financial management, important though that may be; not in reporting mechanisms, important though they may be; not in financing frameworks, important though they may be. The essence of accountability for Crown corporations lies, in the first instance, on the ability of Parliament to control the authority and the mandating for the establishment and creation of a Crown corporation. That is the point.
In the first instance, at birth, is the right and ability of Parliament to hold Crown corporations accountable to the people of this country. It is in the first creation of the Crown corporation that this must be established. I looked at the Bill to see whether or not the Government had taken that first fundamental step. Did the Government in Bill C-24 provide for the important thing? As the Auditor General understands and as everyone understands, the important thing is for Parliament to be able to control the terms of reference for the creation of a Crown corporation. Indeed, that is such an important and fundamental principle that the Minister put it in his press release; he said that Crown corporations should be created by Parliament. The Bill does not clearly state that. It

May 1, 1984
Financial Administration Act
is not honestly exposed by the Government. There are no less than at least four ways, even with this Bill, that Crown corporations can be established without this Parliament even having a look see or a say in it. First, Mr. Speaker, there is no authority in this Bill for this Parliament to have anything to say about the creation of Crown corporations which are subsidiaries of current parent corporations. As anyone knows who has looked at the literature, the biggest proliferation of Crown corporations has been from parent corporations establishing subsidiary corporations. Bill C-24 does not change that one bit. Crown corporations can go on creating subsidiaries as long as they want without reference to this Parliament.
Second, Mr. Speaker, a Crown corporation can be established without reference to this Parliament if its power derives from an already existing Act of Parliament. And there is an already existing Act of Parliament which allows a Crown corporation to be established without having to come to this Parliament. Some of the most enormous Crown corporations can be established that way. That is indisputable. Large Crown corporations can be established without reference to this Parliament simply because there is an ancient authority in an existing Act of Parliament.
That is not true.

It is true. Third, Mr. Speaker, a Crown corporation can be created by a special Bill, and in doing so the Government knew that it had to come to Parliament. That is why, Mr. Speaker, in that part of the Act where it knew it had to come to Parliament, it limited debate. In creating a special Bill where it knew it had to come to Parliament, it decided it was going to limit debate; and if you read the Bill, Mr. Speaker, you will see it has limited debate to seven hours in the House of Commons and to 30 days in committee. Government can create any corporation it likes in a new Bill and this Bill contains a clause which closes down Parliament's ability to debate it beyond seven hours in the House and beyond 30 days in committee.
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, there is still a very open question with which the Government has not yet dealt, and that is whether or not this Bill is stronger than Section 16 of the Interpretation Act which gives prerogatives to the Cabinet to create Crown corporations without reference to Parliament.
Those are four clear examples, Mr. Speaker, within this Bill, which is supposed to control Crown corporations by giving accountability to Parliament, which shows that in fact the Government can establish Crown corporations, or Crown corporations can be established, without reference to Parliament.
The short point, Mr. Speaker, is that this is not a Bill which expands Parliament's rights and ability to control Crown corporations. What it does, Mr. Speaker, is expand the Cabinet's power to run Crown corporations without reference to Parliament. That is what it does. As a matter of fact, on page 22 the Auditor General in his report of 1983 said in the shortest way I know, and it is not changed by the Bill:
Taken together with my earlier words about the Financial Statements of the Government of Canada, the result is-
I underline this to the Minister now in the House:
-nothing less than the fragmentation of the sovereignty of Parliament.
That is exactly what it is, Mr. Speaker, because all that has been talked about is the power of the Cabinet, not the power of Parliament. We have not been talking about the ability of Parliament, acting on behalf of the people of this country, being able to control the power and authority of this Government to deal with Crown corporations.
I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that the establishment of financial and management systems for Crown corporations, of reporting systems and so on, are very important and fundamental to this Bill, and fundamental to everything about this place is the power of government and the ability to control it. Throughout the whole history of parliament, not only this Parliament but of all Westminster parliamentary systems, the rights of the Speaker, my rights as a Member of Parliament, the rights of a Minister and, indeed, all the rights of the people of this country have been linked to the ability of Parliament to control the expenditures of government.
If you read your history, Mr. Speaker, you will find that the most important debates affecting the rights of individuals in this country and the rights of Hon. Members of this House have been directly related to the ability of this House to control the expenditures of the Crown. All the old battles between kings and parliaments were precisely on that point. Our system of parliamentary democracy exists or does not exist on the basis of our ability to limit the power of government. Our ability to limit the power of government rests directly on our ability to control expenditures and hold the government accountable for those expenditures. That is a simple fact of the history of Westminster parliaments.
That is why people attach so much importance to it, and they finally woke up, Mr. Speaker, when they saw us going from eight Crown corporations to over 300 Crown corporations, when they saw us move to $63 billion from the figure in 1962, when they saw the massive change in the power of government with no control by this Parliament. They instinctively know that if the people of this country, through Parliament, cannot control the expenditures of government, and in this instance the Crown corporations, then its ability to control the power of government generally is fundamentally flawed.
People do not pay attention to Parliament, Mr. Speaker, on a daily basis. Some people do but most people do not. They go about their daily affairs, trying to organize their lives as best they can. What they hope will happen, Mr. Speaker, is that the accountability which they assume Parliament has to hold the Government responsible is in place. That is why, Mr. Speaker, in the Final analysis, what we are talking about is not finance. What we are talking about is not finance but the ability of the people of this country to control the power of government through Parliament.
The people know one other thing, Mr. Speaker. They know that this Bill is a whitewash because they know the Govern-
May 1, 1984

ment has had the ability to act responsibly but has not done so. That is the truth of it all. No tinkering with the structure of government, bad as it is, can change the face of a bad and irresponsible government.
The only reason we have this Bill before us is that this Government has been badgered to bring something forward; but it is thin and pale and will not restore the ability of the people of this country to hold this Government accountable through this Parliament.

In typical Liberal fashion, he had to maintain political control by personally appointing the board of directors. He refused to allow open nominations, which would have been one way of circumventing political patronage. He also excluded local municipalities and communities, which are very much affected by local port development, from having any kind of meaningful participation in the policy and planning structures.
Another long established and essential Crown corporation is Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In this instance it seems to me that there is a confusion in roles between the needs of consumers who need affordable housing and should have a right to it in our country and the desires of housing developers who want to make as many bucks as possible by having housing under the control of the private sector, provided, of course, that there are lots of government subsidies and tax write-offs. CMHC is not accountable to the elected Members of this House. There is no housing committee in the House of Commons. There is no place where we can discuss the housing needs and problems of our constituents and of the country as a whole. Housing is a very critical and basic need affecting every family. Surely this is a prime example of a Crown corporation that should be much more accountable not only financially but in the establishment of its goals and priorities for housing programs.
Decent, affordable housing should be the right of Canadians. It should not be left to the whims of bureaucrats or of HUDAC developers to establish housing policy. Yet that is what has happened. There should be long-range planning based on population trends. That is another thing that does not happen. There should be a sound controlled mortgage assistance policy so every time we have a new budget we do not need to have a new program that nobody understands and that lower income people usually cannot use. There should be assured financing for social housing so that societies that are planning housing should not have to do all their planning for a year or two, putting all kinds of effort and funds into initial planning, only to find in the end that there are no funds available.
The development of housing is a social investment. It creates jobs and is an industry that should be stabilized rather than being based on ad hoc programs which vary from one political budget to another. This corporation and the housing industry itself should be accountable to a committee of Parliament to develop sound, long-range non-partisan planning for the future
housing needs of Canadians. Accountability involves more than financial accountability. There must also be accountability for policy objectives and for the quality of service in relation to the social goals and needs of our people.
I want to cite two examples of CMHC policies which have been of considerable concern to this Party and to many of our constituents. As I have pointed out several times in Parliament, CMHC has chosen to ignore the fair wages and hours of labour provisions of the Canada Labour Code as a result of pressure from private, non-union construction firms and the powerful HUDAC lobby. This means that housing societies in Vancouver, which in many cases have been helped by pension funds provided by construction unions, are not allowed themselves to employ union construction firms to build their housing. Highly skilled and experienced union tradespeople are unemployed in very very high numbers in British Columbia, as they are in other parts of Canada, while CMHC, by its policy, prevents housing societies from using union labour and using firms which are unionized.
CMHC and other Crown corporations should be required to adhere to decent labour standards under the fair wages provisions. I was told by CMHC officials that because it was a Crown corporation they did not apply. I think those labour standards should apply. Also, I think policies such as mandatory affirmative action should apply equally in Crown corporations right across the board.
The unfair negative evaluation of CMHC social programs in the news last year is another example of a biased kind of report done by private people with vested interest. This definitely influenced public opinion across Canada very unfairly. We had no chance to hear about this in the House or to have alternate points of view presented in committee. The City of Vancouver had a housing researcher who used the same facts, analysed them and came to a conclusion the opposite to that in the CMHC report, that there should be continued support for co-op and non-profit housing, with some changes perhaps in the application of it. There was no opportunity to hear, as I said, any of these reports or to hear from witnesses from housing societies and co-ops in a committee of the House. There was no chance for us as Members to participate in representing the views and the needs of our constituents. I am pretty sure we have all had practical experience as housing has been very difficult in many areas of Canada.
The negative impact or impression that was left on the public was a great disservice to people who have worked for many many years in housing societies and co-operatives to build affordable housing, who had put in hours and hours of volunteer time and who had developed housing for low and middle income people. Certainly there is room for improvement and modification in most Crown corporations, and CMHC and the non-profit housing program is no exception. This could be done again with sound objective research, wide involvement and with accountability to Parliament and to the public in general.
I do not have time to go into other examples in the time that I have left, Mr. Speaker. I know I have concentrated mostly on
May 1, 1984

the kinds of Crown corporations which relate more to social policies, my area of concern in this caucus as housing critic. However, we all and the public share a very great concern. I think the negative image of Crown corporations is certainly exemplified most in the examples of de Havilland and Cana-dair. 1 am sure most Members have mentioned the $2.6 billion of government funds allocated to these two companies. Executives in de Havilland got bonuses to the tune of $155,000 while workers were laid off. de Havilland spent over $500 million, tax dollars again, to cover its debts for 1983 alone. The CDIC also gave bonuses to seven senior officials to the tune of $82,000. We can go on and on about executives and the gifts they receive.
Another area where more accountability is needed is from the very minister responsible for this situation, a minister who is not elected and is not responsible to this House. We have no way in which to question him. He is like an emperor in British Columbia as the Senator appointed for that territory. He makes decisions with no reference back to democratic government and to committees which should be established in this House.
Finally, in reviewing this Bill I share the concern of other Members. It is unfortunate that we are restricted by imposed time limits. We all agree that changes are needed to make Crown corporations more accountable. There should be regular reviews, not only budget reviews but reviews of programs in terms of the service the people of Canada deserve. The mandate of those corporations should also be reviewed. It is very doubtful that this Bill will allow accountability to Members of Parliament and through us to the people of Canada. It is the people of Canada after all who pay the bill for all Crown corporations, Mr. Speaker. People are also paying in some cases for inefficiency, political expediency, when they should be paying for a much more efficient service.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens).

Mr. Speaker, according to the standard the Hon. Member laid out to the House with respect to whether or not it is necessary or possible to have Crown corporations, could she indicate whether there are any Crown corporations which the federal Government now owns that she feels are dispensable? If so, what are they?

Mr. Speaker, I do not feel, partly because we do not have a way of getting information in this House, that I am the person to evaluate every Crown corporation in Canada. I think that would be pretty presumptuous of me. I have some personal opinions, but I do not have enough data to mention this in the House. I think there should be a way of making evaluations. Most institutions are self-perpetuating, that is the nature of large institutions, but there should be times when some Crown corporations are terminated. What we would be most concerned about is whether they are of value of the people of Canada, whether tax dollars are justified from that point of view and whether they are run efficiently. I think that would be the criteria at which we would look.
Financial Administration Act

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) mentioned that a number of our Crown corporations have become "far too large". Would the Hon. Member agree with the comment that Crown corporations can add personnel more easily to their payrolls than can private industry and that consequently in most of our Crown corporations there is an over-abundance of staff? That was certainly found to be true in Canadair. It had 22 vice-presidents and now it has only 12. They have retired a few and have done away with 338 jobs. This means that 338 people were being paid for their good looks or for some other reason.
If the Hon. Member believes that a Crown corporation can act as efficiently as a private corporation, which is under the control of someone who wants to make a profit from the operation, how would she or her Party control the tendency to increase the number of employees in Crown corporations, because they are being paid, not from a payroll as a result of its operations, but from tax revenues of the country?

Mr. Speaker, I think that is a very valid question. Having worked in a public agency myself, I can say that it is natural, as is the case in the Public Service, for bureaucracies to tend to grow and perpetuate themselves. Therefore we have to build something into the system to reverse this. It does not mean that the purpose of the corporation is invalid or that there is not a need for a particular Crown corporation. There may or may not be a need, but I would think that it comes back to the debate about accountability.
I am not an expert in this area, but if the Government really wanted to improve the situation-and certainly it has a responsibility to see that tax dollars are used efficiently and effectively-there could be an ombudsman service or an auditing service which would have real clout and could make changes. That is why it is important to have more accountability to Parliament or to bodies established for that purpose.

There is another point to which I listened with interest when the Hon. Member was speaking. That was the matter of homes for our people. I do not think there is any disagreement among Hon. Members of the House that we want Canadian families to own their own homes. I assume that is an objective of the NDP as well as of the PCs and the Liberals. In meeting that objective we have to be realistic in terms of setting the final prices of homes. Otherwise we simply bar scores and perhaps even hundreds or thousands of families, particularly young families upon marriage or with small children, from ever buying homes. Some of my own constituents have said that they would love to own homes but that they are unable to accumulate that much money.
Also the Hon. Member mentioned union wages and fair wages. I believe in fair wages, because often union wages are not fair. Plumbers who are charging $18 to $25 per hour shove the price of homes impossibly high so that people cannot buy them. Also there are carpenters who are insisting upon $12 to $16 per hour, whereas others are quite prepared to work for $8

May 1, 1984
Adjournment Motion
or $10 per hour. I believe in fair wages and I believe in unions. However, how does the Hon. Member reconcile keeping the final prices of homes within reach of our people when hourly rates go into the building of homes?

In relation to the first question, while I think there are many Canadians who want to own their own homes, time have changed. It is interesting that in urban settings well over 50 per cent of the people are tenants, many of whom are so by choice. We cannot always think about this question in traditional terms. However, certainly those who have families should have the right to own homes.
When I talked about housing, I talked about shelter in a general sense. That included rental housing and co-operative ownership, which is different but somewhat like a co-operative rental situation. We must have a range of ways for people to accomplish this. We must have fair wages. When we talk about fair wages legislation, it does not mean that people have to unionize if they do not want to. It comes somewhere within the realm of ensuring the payment of sensible and practical wages so that workers are not exploited by getting excessively low wages.
I also referred to housing developments, non-profit developments or co-operatives where larger housing developments are being built and are more deserving of unions. Quite often in the case of individual homes people want to put in some of their own labour. However, there is no question that the role of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation-and this was the point I was attempting to make-should be to develop programs from a long-range point of view, not just this ad hockery. These programs should allow for choices, for people within certain income ranges to get into starter homes with some assistance, and for people who simply do not have downpayments to have co-op housing available to them. It is also very important to have decent rental accommodation, including rental accommodations for people with higher incomes. We are talking about a range of programs, but certainly CMHC should be responsible for them in the interests of Canadians, not in the interests of private developers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: For debate, the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis).
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Chair should have seen the Hon. Member on the government side. I apologize to the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings. The Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson).

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the Hon. Member of the Opposition for standing aside at this particular time.
First, I want to commend the Opposition for having established its task force to look into Crown corporations. Also I commend the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) for the work he did in chairing that task force. I believe this approach, followed through to its logical conclusion by Members of Parliament, will make us all better equipped to deal with the very complex issues that we face. This type of undertaking to develop policy should be made far more on the basis of a House approach, mandated by Parliament. I do not necessarily believe that it should be restricted to the particular Parties in Parliament and be funded by those particular Parties.
Having said that, I find it very difficult to understand why the Hon. Member for Calgary South, in commenting on this particular Bill to regulate and make Crown corporations accountable, said that the Bill was an almost incomprehensible piece of legislative mishmash and gobbledegook. The Bill is very complex. It is not going to be perceived at one glance as solving all of the problems we face with respect to Crown corporations.
On the other hand, the main point I want to make today is that this Bill responds almost measure for measure to the concerns that were raised by the task force of the Official
May 1, 1984

Opposition. It is perhaps not unusual, but very beneficial that the recommendations contained in the provisions of Bill C-24 almost mirror the recommendations put forward by the Opposition task force. These were the two groups researching this issue. They came to almost identical conclusions. This is why this Bill should not be the subject of partisan debate. I believe we should get this Bill into committee as quickly as possible in order that should there be any technical problems inherent in it, we can deal with them on a non-partisan basis, and this House has demonstrated that it is prepared to deal with it on that basis.
I wish to deal with the recommendations of the Tory task force. I will go through them one by one in order to show how we have responded to those concerns and our solution in dealing with them. The first is the requirement for the submission of business plans by Crown corporations, that they be tabled in Parliament and be examined by appropriate parliamentary committees. That is in our Bill.
Second, the Opposition study recommended clarification of the role of the Auditor General in auditing Crown corporations as well as clarifying the relationship of the Auditor General who audits Crown corporations with the private sector auditor. The role of the auditor and the Auditor General is very clearly set out in this Bill. This is what we have done. I might also add that we went to considerable lengths to weigh carefully the views and the recommendations made over the past years, not only by the Auditor General but also by the Public Accounts Committee and the Lambert Commission. In essence, we have chosen to follow Lord Macauley's famous dictum, namely, choose wisely, consult liberally. I know the "consult liberally" aspect of this dictum might be anathema to the Opposition, but I suggest that that is the way, through consultation, and through careful study that is epitomized in the results of this Bill. That is the way in which we have been able to come to the conclusions we have arrived at.
The third aspect of the Tory report calls for improved accounting procedures and practices. Our Bill sets out, in a way that matches the view of the Opposition task force, the concerns about ways of improving accounting procedures and practices. We go one step further. We take the additional step of requiring by legislation that statements set out information clearly and in accordance with the major businesses or activities of each Crown corporation. In other words, we are using a new type of accounting approach for Crown corporations whereby each of their individual businesses, even if they are all contained within one corporate shell, have to be accounted for separately. That was not the generally accepted accounting practice previously.
With regard to some of the remaining recommendations of the Opposition task force, you will find slight differences between our approach and that adopted by the Opposition. I am prepared to elaborate on these differences at the present time, but because they are largely technical in nature, I believe they would be best resolved without polemics in the House and on television. We should sit down in committee and work through these areas in a very non-partisan manner. Since we
Financial Administration Act
are not there, and with the emphasis on trying to get us there sooner, let me deal with these points.
First, the Opposition seeks a rationalization in the relationship of Crown corporations to the Government based on a return to effective, individual ministerial responsibility. We have done this. Each Crown corporation is the specific responsibility of a Minister who is available in this House. Each Crown corporation is that Minister's responsibility to account for to this Parliament. A Minister can be called to account publicly at any time in this House for every one of our Crown corporations.
I am wondering what the implication is of the criticism of the Opposition. Is it that there should be only one Member, whoever looks at the financial statements, business plans or ideas of a Crown corporation? We do not feel that that is realistic. We do not know of any system in the world where only one Minister is involved in looking at the business plan and in paying attention to the public policy aspect inherent in Crown corporations or in any particular Crown corporation. For example, why should the designated responsible Minister not be able to consult with the Minister of Finance, the President of the Treasury Board, the Prime Minister, or even the whole Cabinet, on particular issues affecting Crown corporations? It is only good advice. It is good practice to seek the advice and recommendations of other Ministers, particularly those who have a particular concern about a Crown corporation.
In our Bill we have clarified this relationship between the Government and the Crown corporation and strengthened the existing system whereby an individual Minister is designated for each parent Crown corporation. The role of the Government per se is clarified. Surely that must have been what the Opposition was seeking. Why then the hassle on these particular provisions?
Another area where the disagreement is more rhetoric than actual is the classification system, the way in which we have classified Crown corporations as to whether they have largely a social or commercial purpose, whether or not they are in competition with the private sector, and the way we have scheduled those Crown corporations. Our approach has been to segregate the commercially-oriented Crown corporations according to the extent to which they are exposed to competition from the private sector. That makes eminent good sense. If the Crown corporation is competing with the private sector in a particular area, why should that Crown corporation not have some of the advantages in a competitive marketplace that the private sector corporation has?
This does not necessarily mean that there should be a Crown corporation in an area which is being adequately served by the private sector. It does not mean that we as a government want to hold on to our Crown corporations. In fact, in a companion Bill before Parliament dealing with the Canada Development Investment Corporation, part of the specific mandate is articulated there. The Government is to continue the policies of trying to dispose of Crown corporations which are no longer essential to the public purposes and to the service of public

May 1, 1984
Financial Administration Act
needs in Canada. That is one area in which I think the Official Opposition and the Government would find accord and harmony. Again, there is no reason for bickering or hassling.
Another area in which I believe the apparent differences between the Government and the Opposition are more perceived than real is that with respect to the acquisitions and new incorporations of Crown corporations; in other words, the establishment of new Crown corporations to undertake certain activities. We have proposed that the Government be permitted to incorporate a parent Crown corporation under the Canada Business Corporations Act.
In some cases, one would have to agree with members of the Opposition who say that it would be most appropriate if there were to be a special Act of Parliament passed such as the ones which have been passed before for large operations such as the CN when establishing a new Crown corporation. However, why should every new Crown corporation need to go through that type of legislative parliamentary scrutiny when most Crown corporations fall under the umbrella of one of the following four Crown corporations; CN, Air Canada, Canada Development Corporation and Petro-Canada?
I hope that Hon. Members are trying to introduce a degree of private-sector accountability into the decision-making processes of Crown corporations. That type of accountability is critical. However, why should an airline not be able to hive off some of its operations into a separate Crown corporation for business reasons only?
In order for us to use a Canada Business Corporations Act type of subsidiary corporation, there are constraints which must be met. First, that subsidiary corporation must fall within the overall mandate of the Crown corporation itself. It cannot go on a new lark and it cannot go from widgets into doughnuts. That is one type of control which we have and we still require that the Crown corporation receive the consent of Parliament. The matter would automatically be referred to a parliamentary committee for 30 sitting days, and then an opportunity would be afforded for at least seven hours of debate in the House before the new corporation is established.
I know what kind of constructive work can be done in 30 sitting days by a parliamentary committee that is dedicated to making things work rather than one which is hell-bent on electoral gains and political advantage. That is one very responsible measure. When we are speaking about seven hours of debate in the House as an additional control on the establishment of Crown corporations, we are speaking of at least two full days' debate. I ask if we really do need to impose that type of shackle on a corporation such as Air Canada, which might want to hive off some of its tourist-generating activities into a subsidiary corporation for accounting and management structure purposes. The private sector has no such constraints; yet we have put these constraints on our own ability to act in this area.
I am prepared to listen to reasonable arguments from the other side and I believe that they would best be heard in
committee. I am prepared to hear why these safeguards are not adequate, particularly when referring to corporations which fall under Part II of Schedule C such as the big ones which compete with the private sector in various areas.
Another area on which the Tory task force recommended clarification was that of the responsibilities of directors and officers. The issue involving the appointment of officers, directors and chairpersons of federal agencies and boards is one which our task force on regulatory reform looked at very candidly and very thoroughly. Three members of the Opposition were members of that task force and we came to the unanimous conclusion that full public scrutiny by subjecting appointments to congressional debates, like those which occur in the United States is not the proper way to go. We felt that there is a better way to go in terms of appointments. We suggested that anyone should be entitled to recommend people who would be competent to fill particular positions. However, we felt that after consultations, it must in the end be the decision of the responsible Minister. This decision would be made after consultations and after soliciting a public list of names. That conclusion received unanimous Opposition approval from members of both the NDP and the Conservative Party.
There are very good reasons why it should be the Government that appoints directors of Crown corporations. The Government is the shareholder. It is the body which is responsible to the Canadian people. It is the trustee for the Canadian people. If we as a Government cannot act to remove the directors who manage and control a Crown corporation, then how can we say that we are responsible? How can the Minister stand up in the House and say that he is responsible? How can Opposition Members pin down anyone on this side of the House with respect to a Crown corporation if we do not have the ability to control those who are responsible for management and control on our behalf? We in turn must act as trustees for the public interest.
Through this Bill, Mr. Speaker, we are striving for control, direction and accountability. I fail to understand how this can be achieved without the Government having the ability to appoint directors and chief executive officers.
Another aspect of this Bill of which I am very proud is the fact that we have control over the remuneration received by those directors and chief executive officers. In my opinion, that is critical because there are times in our public lives when we cannot have increases in wages and salaries being paid to executive officers of particular Crown corporations.
Or bonuses to de Havilland.

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but I must inform him that his time has expired. Are there questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, I would like the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) to answer one question. How can the president of a Crown corporation be held accountable? If a board of directors has any role to play in a Crown
May 1, 1984

corporation at all, how can that board hold the president of a Crown corporation accountable if, in effect, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) makes the appointment? Could he answer that simple question for me?

Mr. Speaker, if what we are trying to do is to invite a comparison between the public sector involved in the control of a Crown corporation and the shareholders of a private corporation, then there is something I would like to say about that. In a private corporation other than a Crown corporation, shareholders or investors are the ones who elect the directors to act on their behalf. In a private corporation such as a Canada business corporation, an Ontario business corporation and, I would venture to say, even an Alberta corporation, there are certain times at which the shareholders are entitled to act and to undertake by resolution certain responsibilities. This is particularly true with a corporation whose shares are not widely held. There are provisions in the law whereby the shareholders, for whom the directors are merely trustees acting on their behalf, can undertake that direct responsibility. To me, entering into the role of being able to appoint a chief executive officer is merely by-passing the role of the directors and going directly to the people for whom those officers are working. That is a power which we have under this particular law.
I fail to see how that differs from a closely held corporation in the private sector. There is no difference whatsoever. As a matter of fact, what it does is to allow the type of accountability which Hon. Members opposite have been talking about. It allows us to act very quickly if the chief executive officer is botching it up. Then we do not have to call a directors' meeting in order to dismiss that individual. There might be times when we would want that to take place.

That, Mr. Speaker, is exactly the point. The Hon. Member has just confirmed it. What is a board of directors for then? I am quite prepared to admit that there is a vast difference between a multi-shareholder company and a single shareholder company such as we have in a Crown corporation. But, as the Hon. Member has just said, if need be the board will be by-passed. Therein lies the problem. That is exactly what happened in the case of Canadair. The directors served no purpose whatsoever. My point is: Why have them? Why resort to the subterfuge?

Mr. Speaker, the directors can play a very valuable role in a corporation. I do not know whether in the Hon. Member's business life he had a lot of outside directors in his corporation, but if he did he would realize that they performed many more functions other than just choosing the chief executive officer. As a shareholder of a corporation, I am sure that he would have indicated to the directors who he wanted to serve as the chief executive officer. Forget the sham. We are laying it right there. The chief executive officer will be accountable to the people of Canada, the shareholders of the
Financial Administration Act
corporation, through the Minister. That is not a sham; it is calling a spade a spade. It is putting the responsibility there.
The Hon. Member mentioned Canadair. The trouble was that the directors were by-passed. By-passed by whom? Members on this side of the House agree that what happened with Canadair was a disgrace. We did not have the type of instrument in Parliament to supervise adequately what was going on. We as the shareholders did not have the type of business strcuture, such as is proposed in the CDIC Bill, that could give us instant results. It can place before Parliament, very quickly, quarterly results of Crown corporations such as we are proposing so that we as Members acting for the shareholders, the public of Canada, can perform the watch-dog interest that is critical.
I want to ensure, and I think it is shown by the board of the CDIC which is proposed, that we are setting up a good structure which will adhere to sound business principles and which will have a blue chip board of directors-people with proven competence in business areas; people with proven competence in running big businesses in many sectors in Canada. That is why I would like to see the CDIC Bill as a companion Bill to this one.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues across the way. I do not really mind if there are no questions; that does not bother me at all. I will certainly try to stay well within the 20 minutes.
In dealing with Bill C-24, as my colleagues have done, I intend to be critical of the Bill. It seems to me that this is indeed another example of the state of the Government in that we have had, over the past number of months, indeed over the last few years, a number of Bills brought before us that have been rushed in, have been deficient in make-up and not really

May 1, 1984
Financial Administration Act
ready to be presented to the House. I had hoped to spend a few moments dealing with some statistics, but my colleague from Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), who was very eloquent in that area, did a good job. I intend to get involved only in one statistic that my colleague from Rosedale did not cover, that is a statistic having to do with special enterprises. I quote the following from a recent article in The Financial Post which reads:
Statistics Canada publishes data on what it calls government enterprises- "agencies engaged primarily in operations of a commercial or industrial nature, which either compete actively with similar operations in the private sector or monopolize activities that would otherwise be carried out in the private sector."
In 1981, this description fitted 155 federal agencies and subsidiaries (total assets: $50.9 billion);
These were the agencies which compete with private industry and, in fact, to continue the quotation:
-there are six of these animals among the top 50 non-financial firms ranked by The Post, ranging from Canadian Wheat Board (number nine) to Air Canada (number 35)-
I intend to quote fairly extensively someone who is well known to my colleagues on the other side of the House. I thought I would use an article by Mr. Paul E. Martin, son of a former illustrious Member of this House and now President and Chief Executive Officer of The CSL Group Incorporated, simply because if I were to use entirely original material in speaking to this Bill this afternoon, I am sure I would have a great deal of criticism and comments from my colleagues opposite. It seems to me that if I quote to them from what was said by one of their own people, perhaps it will carry some weight with them.
Was he ever a Member of the House?

Mr. Martin has the qualifications of the Liberal Party at his back and there is no question about that. I will be quoting some excerpts from an article written by Mr. Martin in a publication called Policy Options of March, 1984. While I will not, of course, try to deal with the whole article, nonetheless it will not change the thrust. Let me begin with a very brief quote from Mr. Martin's article. He says this:
Governments are by nature slow in seizing opportunities, facing up to changing conditions, or simply correcting mistakes.
He goes on to say:
Indeed, it would not be unreasonable to suggest that one of the reasons for the unwarranted expansion in the activities of Crown corporations arises from governments' attempt to shortcircuit Parliament in the development of policy.
Is this why, Mr. Speaker, as others have said, and in particular my colleague, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), that this legislation does not cover 109 Crown corporations mixed with joint enterprises and their subsidiaries? Is this also why we have a dearth of regulations in this particular piece of legislation? My colleagues have all pointed out, Mr. Speaker, and I do not intend to repeat it, the lack of regulations available to us and the continual reference in this piece of legislation to regulations. The fact is that the Bill relies entirely on regulations, and we have no idea what those
regulations will be. This is not the first time we have been faced with that situation in this House, and when we have been faced with that sort of thing, we found to our grief that when the regulations did come out, they did not bear much resemblance to what we felt was the intent of the particular legislation.
I want to deal again briefly with Mr. Martin's article. He goes on to say, and I quote:
It is difficult to envisage a circumstance in which Crown corporations can be as efficient as private sector companies. Not that the latter are models by any means. But, lacking some of the inherent advantages and political constraints of Crowns, private enterprise is forced to be more disciplined, and hence more cost effective.
Do we really believe, Mr. Speaker, that the post office in attempting to get into the retail business is going to be effective? Is it going to pay taxes comparable to other merchants in small communities? Is it going to use tax free trucking to carry the merchandise back and forth? Is it, indeed, going to attempt to hide the inefficiency of the post office by getting itself involved in competition with small businessmen? Obviously, that is an area which all of us must decry.
Let me quote again from Mr. Martin, and I said I was going to quote fairly extensively from the article in order to make my point. He said the following:
And government owned companies possess some very powerful advantages.
First, Crowns operate and invest without fear of bankruptcy in the knowledge that government will not let them go under. This in turn enables their managements to engage in programs in which the cost incurred may well be disproportionate to the benefits gained but which nonetheless result in a major long-term advantage over private sector competitors who are more subject to short-term cash flow fluctuations.
I ask the non-rhetorical question, Mr. Speaker, of my colleagues across the way: How many of you know companies in your constituencies which would be successful if money were available, if it were not a problem; if agencies like the Federal Business Development Bank would provide funds to no end; if there were guarantees from federal agencies; if Revenue Canada were not on their backs trying to put them out of business? If, indeed, that was not a problem, how many companies in your constituencies would in the long run make a profit? I suggest to you, Sir, that in my own constituency I can think of at least a dozen which have had some very serious difficulties, and if they could have had unlimited resources for the first two or three years there is no question but that over the long haul they would have made money. Going back to Mr. Martin again, he said:
-Crown corporations have superior access to government and thus the greater ability to influence government policy that affects them. Indeed, it is not unusual for their personnel to be drawn from the very bureaucracy which has the final policy say over industries in which the private and public sectors compete.
On the Order paper I have a number of questions regarding the Savin Corporation which buys photocopiers from Japan and resells them. It was purchased by the CDC when it was losing money. It is now in the market selling below cost, competing unfairly with other companies which either produce or buy and resell photocopiers. Yet, how many government corporations do we fund today using the Savin photocopiers? I
May 1, 1984

know that my constituency and the surrounding area are flooded with them. I assume the same is true in other constituencies. I doubt that mine would be an exception. I assume the same is true in Ottawa and other areas. Certainly, to have access to the Government is a very real benefit to a Crown corporation. Quoting again from Mr. Martin, he said:
I would suggest that, as the need for Crown corporations to spearhead frontier development declines and the need for commercial discipline becomes paramount, the time has come to consider privatization of mature Crown corporations.
I want to make a point here, Mr. Speaker, that I am now getting into an area which I am personally advocating. The task force, which was very effectively headed by the Hon. Member for Calgary South and the Senator from the other place, has not dealt with this particular question. The excellent report of the task force left out this particular area of privatization. I think it felt that its terms of reference did not go that far. I suggest that I would like to see some privatization of our Crown corporations. I go back to Mr. Martin to make my next point. He said, and I quote:
It is important to emphasize that privatization in no way detracts from the national symbolism of the institutions concerned. They would still be as much Canadian as if owned by the government. The major difference would be that ownership, instead of being concentrated in the hands of a government elite, would be spread out among the Canadian public. In fact, it can be argued that government is so large and so remote that people have difficulty regarding its ownership as their ownership.
There have been some comments made by different speakers, particularly from the New Democratic Party, having to do with the actions of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), when he formed the Government, regarding PetroCan. I believe it is fair to say today, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians by and large recognize finally that PetroCan is much the same as other major oil companies in that it charges as much, is involved in price wars, and is selling service stations. They do not feel the personal relationship, which has been suggested through advertising, with that Crown corporation. That Crown corporation, they now realize, is not making money, is building itself an empire and is generally acting irresponsibly, as many Crown corporations do where there is not sufficient restriction.
I would like to go back to Mr. Martin's article for one last time to help me make my point with regard to privatization. Mr. Martin said, and I quote:
The advantages to be derived by privatization, wherever possible, are powerful.
First, it eliminates the twin problems of Crown corporation lack of accountability and crowding out of the private sector by the simple expedient of joining the private sector and accepting the discipline of the market place.
Second, it would force government to be explicit in its policy directives. Crown corporations are too often used either as a means of developing policy outside of Parliament's scrutiny or as a means of avoiding the making of a policy altogether.
All of this having been said, however, the... most important reason for privatization arises from the opportunity cost of tying up scarce financial resources in well established Crown corporations, once the original public policy objectives have been met. Important new policy initiatives are being forsworn because of a lack of funding. Does it make any sense to tie up billions of dollars
Financial Administration Act
in mature Crowns while turning our backs, to an important degree, on entrepreneurs who would develop new technologies and people who would benefit from new or further training?
I could go on at some length dealing with those other parts of Bill C-24, Mr. Speaker. I could deal with the loopholes that, as my colleague from Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) said, prevent Parliament from dealing with Crown corporations. I could deal with the fact that there will be less information available and continuing problems with the Attorney General. However, the fact is that Bill C-24 is just not adequate.
I will not go into great detail on this, but I would like to mention a problem that I spent hours debating in the House about one and a half or two years ago. A Crown corporation headed by the man who is now the head of VIA Rail was determined to buy equipment from Japan. I questioned the Government, the Minister and the head of the Harbours Board. I pointed out, and was never challenged, that the equipment in question had never before been made by any other company than the one in my constituency. The company in my constituency had bid low, had met the delivery dates, and in fact could do a better job than any other company in the world. Yet this Crown corporation gave a $20 million contract to Japan. Shortly thereafter, in another bid in South America, the Belleville company was successful. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, patently absurd that we would have a Canadian Crown corporation buying offshore, having all the advantages to buy from a Canadian company, while foreign companies on another continent recognize the expertise of the Canadian company.
That is an example, Mr. Speaker, of a need for new thoughts, ideas and approaches. It is a need, Mr. Speaker, for a new Government. If the Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) were in the House now, I would say to him through you that the polls suit me just fine. Let us have an election, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have an opportunity to address Bill C-24 in the short amount of time remaining this afternoon. As I am faced with dealing with my remarks within a 10 minute time-table, I would like to zero in specifically on the lack of regulations. By that I mean the fact that the Government has brought in Bill C-24 and has not given the Opposition any opportunity to review the regulations which are going to play such a major part in the actual functioning of Bill C-24. We have not seen them. The Bill gives wide regulations-making power to the Government. We would like to know exactly what the form and content of those regulations will be.
I refer, Mr. Speaker, to Clause 95(10) in which, by regulation, the Government intends to classify major business activity. I refer to Clause 97 which will, by regulation, apply Bill C-24 to subsidiaries. I refer to Clause 101(7) whereby the Government can deal with incorporation and acquisition of subsidiaries by regulation. I refer to Clause 102(2) where, by regulation, subsidiaries and Crown corporations can be exempted from Section 101. I refer to Clause 108(4) where, by regulation, the Government will regulate how agent companies

May 1, 1984
Financial Administration Act
may sell or dispose of property. I refer to Clause 118(3) which defines remuneration. I refer to Clause 124(4) which defines, by regulation, the form and content of the exemption of by-laws from Clause 124. I refer to Clause 130(7) which describes circumstances requiring the approval of corporate plans by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). I refer to Clause 134 wherein the Treasury Board will set the form and content of corporate plans and also set the form, content and timing of operating budgets. I refer to Clause 131(2) wherein Treasury Board may require operating budgets from any C-I corporation. I refer to clause 132(1) wherein Treasury Board may exempt any C-I corporation from requirement to submit a capital budget. I refer to Clause 132(2) wherein C-II corporations may be directed by Treasury Board or the appropriate Minister to submit capital budgets. I refer to Clause 132(4) wherein Treasury Board can approve spending items beyond the budget year. I refer to Clause 132(8) wherein the Minister of Finance may require his approval for a capital budget. I refer to Clause 135(4) wherein the Minister of Finance may exempt a Crown corporation from Clause 135. This clause defines what transactions involve borrowing and specifies the manner of granting approval under Clause 135. I refer to Clause 139(6). This clause troubles me considerably, Mr. Speaker. Therein Treasury Board may prescribe regulations for the preparation of financial statements and supplement or augment generally accepted accounting principles.
Some two years ago, Mr. Speaker, we engaged in a pretty hot and heavy debate in the House. We were able to dissuade the Government from trying to set generally accepted accounting principles by regulation. As a chartered accountant and a fellow of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Ontario, I object very strenuously to any government trying, by regulation, to set generally accepted accounting principles. That is for the profession of accounting to do. The Government has no business doing that. It has no business telling doctors how to take out an appendix. It may be in the business of allowing professions to self-regulate, but once again the Government is trying to set generally accepted accounting principles by regulation. As a professional, I object.
By Clause 142(5) the Governor in Council intends to set regulations prescribing how auditors will be selected. By Clause 152(4) the Treasury Board may make regulations on the form and content of annual reports. In these latter three cases, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the regulations go far beyond what the House can approve.
I would respectfully suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we call it five o'clock. Within the time limit available to me I have tried to keep my speech specifically on the subject of regulations, and thereby tell why we are specifically objecting to the regulation-making part of the Bill. I ask that I be permitted to continue the next time this Bill is brought up in the House.

A motion should be neither argumentative, nor in the style of a speech, nor contain unnecessary provisions or objectionable words.
