subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REDUCING NUCLEAR WEAPONS AND RESUMING DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should call upon the nuclear powers to seek a temporary freeze by all nations on the testing, production and deployment of nuclear weapons and delivery systems pending a genuine reduction in nuclear arsenals, and for the early resumption of negotiations on a treaty for comprehensive disarmament under enforceable world law, which should include:
1.	disarmament by all nations to the level of arms required for internal security;
2.	an international inspection organization able to monitor disarmament and detect violations of the agreement, using both satellites and on-site inspection;
3.	a world peace force able to enforce disarmament and prevent international aggression, the members of which should be individually recruited;
4.	an effective system of world courts and arbitration tribunals; and
5.	a world development fund through which a fixed proportion of the resources made available through disarmament will be devoted to development in the poorest nations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the subject of the motion that I put before the House today, seconded by my colleague from Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), is, in essence, human survival. Its substance is a series of concrete proposals to establish an international climate that is co-operative rather than confrontational, that recognizes that international security must rest in a commitment to joint survival rather than in the threat of mutual destruction, and one that ultimately reduces the risk of a nuclear holocaust.
The motion which is before the House in my name today calls for the Canadian Government to press for an immediate freeze by all nations on the testing, production and deployment of nuclear weapons and their delivery systems. This is to be followed by the resumption of negotiations on a treaty for general disarmament under a reliable system of enforceable world law.
This motion underlines the deep concern felt by members within all Parties and which is reflected by the Canadian public in public marches, referendums and many other public illustrations of concern. It is a concern that the deteriorating state of international relations brought about by nuclear weaponry is so great it is a cause not only for alarm but for a call for action that is being heard across the country.
I need not review before the House the horrific statistics that indicate the probability of nuclear war or the absolute destructive power that nuclear weapons possess. Let me simply say that these facts point to one fundamental conclusion: the risk of extinction is not just one more item on the agenda of issues that face us as parliamentarians today. The life and death of every human being on earth and every future human being transcends all other issues that are on our parliamentary schedule and those of other nations. Surely we can agree on this much.
Less than two generations after the carnage of the Second World War, the world is marching toward the brink of a new abyss, toward a conflict whose consequences would exceed experience and defy imagination. It is not enough for us to
Disarmament
remind ourselves that nuclear war is horrible and to assure ourselves that we are not for extinguishing mankind. Immediate steps must be taken to transfer our security reliance from the nuclear weapons system to another universally accepted system.
Kurt Waldheim, a former Secretary General of the United Nations, argued in his 1980 report on nuclear weapons as follows:
-Only a system of international security, based on the observation of the principles of the United Nations Charter and of other universally accepted instruments of international law, can provide a mutually acceptable basis of security. This must be, therefore, the goal on the road to disarmament. The Charter and nuclear weapons date their existence from the same time. The future road should point to a full reliance on the Charter, and the elimination of all nuclear weapons.
The present motion is unique, and in an important sense, historic. It has been introduced in the Congress of the United States of America. Within a few months it will have been introduced into the Parliaments of Australia, India, Italy, Jamaica, Kenya, New Zealand, Nigeria, the United Kingdom and the European Parliament.
The initiative has been proposed by Parliamentarians for World Order. It is the first time that legislators around our globe have risen simultaneously and, in unison, introduced concrete proposals for peace. It is my opinion, and that of 800 of my parliamentary colleagues on every continent, that this motion outlines the minimum requirements for humanity's survival.
Some Hon. Members will say that the proposals contained in this motion are unrealistic. They are not. Those who believe that we can carry on for another fifty or a hundred years with a system of nation states, arming themselves with ever more lethal weapons, while the earth is depleted of its resources and millions starve, are only fooling themselves. A realistic look at the requirements for human survival must lead us to seek reform of our international system.
The nuclear powers today possess approximately 50,000 nuclear weapons. These weapons have the destructive power of more than one million Hiroshima bombs. The risk of nuclear war is real. It could be triggered by accident. The Accident Measures Agreement, signed in 1971 by the United States and the Soviet Union, states:
-despite the most elaborate precautions, it is conceivable that technical malfunction or human failure, a misinterpreted incident or unauthorized action, could trigger a nuclear disaster or nuclear war.
On at least three occasions in the last two years, American nuclear forces were placed on alert: twice because of the malfunctioning of a computer chip in the North American Air Defence Command's warning system; and once when a test tape depicting a missile attack was inadvertently inserted in the system.
A nuclear war could begin through the escalation of conventional conflict. There are suggestions today that in the Iran-Iraq conflict it may be as close as two years from now when nuclear weaponry is introduced into that conflict. President

May 1, 1984
Disarmament
Kennedy himself stated that the odds on the Cuban missile crisis leading to a full-scale nuclear exchange were about one out of three or even. Fear that the world would be held by terrorists should the nuclear capacity fall into their hands, cannot be dismissed as irrational, Mr. Speaker. Imagine for a moment if Libya had had this capacity during the past several weeks in that tense situation with Great Britain. While there may be only a small probability of a nuclear war this year, it is a fact that over a sufficiently long period of time the probability of nuclear war must approach statistical certainty. We cannot maintain the atomic arsenals we have indefinitely and survive. Sooner or later, something will go wrong.
While it is impossible to know with certainty that a full-scale nuclear war will end human life on this planet, most experts have concluded that the long-term impact of radioactive fallout and the ecological effects, when added to the short-term effects of blast and fire, will end life as we know it. From inside the political and military system, there are voices of warning in the world today, including that of Ambassador George Kennan, Secretary Robert MacNamara, and Admiral Robert Falls.
Talk of a "limited" or winnable nuclear war is ludicrous. Two questions demand answers. We must ask, at what point will the escalation stop? If generals, diplomats and politicians are not able to prevent a nuclear war from starting, can we expect that they will be able to stop it once it has begun?
The late general, Lord Louis Mountbatten of Burma, said shortly before his death:
-the nuclear arms race has no military purpose. Wars cannot be fought with nuclear weapons. There can be no victory. Their existence only adds to our perils because of the illusions (of security) that they generate.
The key advantage of the freeze proposal that I have put before the Canadian House of Commons today is its common-sense simplicity. At one stroke, it would cut through the tangle of technical complexity that has frustrated many arms control efforts. Senator Mark Hatfield, Republican co-sponsor of the freeze resolution in the U.S. Congress, stressed this:
-the moratorium concept has the inestimable political virtue of simplicity. Its benefits to mankind are readily apparent to all and sundry rather than only to a handful of scientists and strategic analysts. There would be no mistaking the moral implications of an agreement to stop the arms race. To a world now cowering in the face of the awesome dangers and technological complexities of the arms race, a moratorium would symbolize hope.
A freeze would forestall a dangerous new round of superpower weapons systems, such as the MX missile and a new Soviet intercontinental missile. Given their astonishing accuracy, these weapons will push both sides toward a "launch-on-warning" nuclear response.
A freeze would prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons to an increasing number of countries, such as Libya, a country which I just mentioned.
Unlike other arms control measures, a freeze would stop the nuclear arms race and set the stage for disarmament.
It will be said by opponents of the freeze that it is unacceptable because the "other side" is ahead. But we can agree that nuclear weapons are different from other weapons. More
bombs do not necessarily mean more strength. When each side can destroy the other many times over, words like "ahead" and "behind" lose their meaning. Congressman James Leach, a Republican from Iowa, illustrates this point in his intervention in the American forum as follows:
-The problem with the logic of those who would reject a freeze, in favour of unrestrained weapons development until an idealized treaty is negotiated, is that their position hinges on the assumption that more nuclear weapons really matter. Death is death. A human being cannot die twice. If two rivals are locked in a small room in a duel to the death where one has 1,400 pistols and the other 1,200, the one with 1,400 has no advantage when one or both parties are likely to be killed or maimed with the first pistol used-
While a nuclear weapons freeze would set the stage for disarmament, nothing short of comprehensive disarmament will ensure our survival. Only by removing the atomic weapons can we remove the threat of nuclear holocaust. Yet as long as the risk of war remains, the nuclear powers will not give up their arsenals. It will be said that talk of general disarmament is idealistic. We must, however, come to grips with general disarmament under world law, if we wish to be realistic about having a world to pass on to future generations. Nations must give up the right to wage war. That is the minimum necessary for survival.
Shridath Ramphal, Secretary-General of the Commonwealth, speaking a few weeks ago to the consultation of National Voluntary Organizations in Ottawa, touched on this theme when he said:
-Nurtured as we are on the doctrine of the nation state, and the concept of national sovereignty which sustains it, we so easily fail to catch a glimpse of the world as a whole.
The sovereignty of all nations in the nuclear age rests in Moscow and Washington. We will only regain our Canadian sovereignty, and other nations will only regain their sovereignty, when the superpowers relinquish the power to annihilate mankind.
To achieve lasting disarmament, four institutions are essential. They are outlined in my motion before the House today. First, an international inspection organization. If nations disarm, they must know that their adversaries are doing likewise. No man will pull down his pants, bend over, and hope someone passing by will resist kicking him. Second, an international police force is necessary. If nations are to reduce the size of their military forces, they must have an alternative on which they can rely for their security. The global police force must be strong enough to enforce two world laws-that no nation may invade another nation and that no nation may rearm. This needs to be enforced.
Third, an improved world judicial system is needed. If nations are to renounce the battlefield as a place to settle disputes, they must have an alternative. Fourth, a world development fund to redirect resources from the arms race to development is needed. To disarm, nations must have security, and there cannot be security in a world where half the population is hungry. This motion recognizes these four insti-
May 1, 1984

tutions as cornerstones of an interdependent global community.
After 30 years, superpower negotiations have reduced neither the quantity of weapons nor their destructive power. The negotiations have provided a stage on which a global audience views its own powerlessness. At present those negotiations, however tenuous, have ceased altogether. Thus we are at a very critical juncture. We must find an alternative approach to the arms race. This is what the marchets in our cities are saying, this is what the municipal-based referendums are saying, this is what the vigils are saying, and this is what the worship services are saying across the country.
President Eisenhower wrote to an American publisher on April 4, 1956 making a crystal-clear point. He said:
When we get to the point, as we one day will, that in any outbreak of general hostilities, regardless of the element of surprise, destruction will be both reciprocal and complete, possibly we will have enough sense to meet at the conference table with the understanding that the era of armaments has ended and the human race must conform its actions to this truth or die.
In concluding my comments in support of my motion before the House today, I invite Hon. Members on all sides to join with me in support of this motion for human survival.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REDUCING NUCLEAR WEAPONS AND RESUMING DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, as chairperson for the Parliamentarians for World Order in Canada, I am pleased to rise and support this proposal. As the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) stated, the substance of this resolution was initiated by the Parliamentarians for World Order internationally.
I would like to make a few brief comments about that organization. It is an international organization of legislators working for disarmament, development and strengthened world institutions. The organization now has over 600 Members of Parliament or legislators in 31 countries. This resolution, which in different words has been called "the call for global survival", has been sent to Members of Parliament around the world, for a total of 25,000 letters to 115 countries in 10 different languages.
It is unfortunate that we must debate such important questions as the freeze on nuclear weapons, and a means to deal with international conflict with so little interest in the House and with so little input from Members. That is partly due to our rules in this Chamber and partly due to our Constitution. However, it is my hope that the debate this afternoon might at least stimulate or encourage the Government to permit a wider debate on these issues which are of such great concern to Canadians. I think we were all struck by the immense numbers of Canadians last weekend who marched in the streets because of their concern about nuclear war; I think there were over
100,000	in Vancouver.
1 know other Hon. Members want to speak, so I will not take much time. However, I want to put on the record some facts with respect to the threat of war today and over the last few years. People have a tendency to forget or to bury their heads in the sand and think that such things will not happen.
Disarmament
Since 1945, since the end of the so-called Second World War, there have been 66 regional wars throughout the world, wherein more than 9 million non-military persons were killed and another 6 million military personnel were killed, for a total of 15 million in 66 wars since 1945.
In 1982, the nations of the world spent more than $650 billion on armaments. That is equal to the total Gross National Product of Latin America and Africa. Of this amount, $100 billion was spent on the production of nuclear arms, which now number 50,000. In contrast to that, the moneys required in the world to provide adequate food, housing, health care and education amount to only $18.5 billion. I say only $18.5 billion when compared with the $650 billion spent on armaments. What a pity, what a shame!
In the United States today, 53 per cent of every tax dollar is spent on military expenditures. That is the greatest percentage in the history of the United States during peacetime. Thirty-five percent of all world armaments are produced in that country, and the 50,000 nuclear weapons which now exist in the world have one million times the destructive power of the explosion at Hiroshima. Imagine that, if you can. The nuclear arms existing in the world today have the capacity to wipe out or destroy 800 million lives in one day. If a nuclear war were to start at the beginning of the day, before the end of that day 800 million lives could be destroyed. Turning to another point, the world now spends 2,300 times more for military activities than for peace activities. I just wanted to put those facts on the record because they are very relevant to the resolution introduced by our colleague today.
Since I want to give other Members a chance to support and talk on this resolution, I will simply say that when we have
50,000	nuclear bombs with a destructive power one million times the Hiroshima bomb which can virtually destroy the world, certainly the only alternative is disarmament and arms control.
I said at the beginning of my remarks that I regretted the fact that we carry on this debate with so little interest in this Parliament. It is too bad we cannot have a process or procedure whereby we could vote on these issues as we did with capital punishment. In that case it was a free vote because we were dealing with life and death issues, something very close to the conscience of Members of Parliament. Here we are dealing with something which could destroy 800 million lives, and we have to deal with it in a process like this. I think that is a very unfortunate set of events. It is too bad that we cannot do what was done in the United States which has so-called non-binding resolutions. The Senate of the United States passed a resolution in favour of a nuclear freeze. It expressed the will of the members of the Senate but it had no binding force on the President. At least the people of the United States knew where their members stood. I wish we could do that in this House. If we cannot do it tonight, let us have an opportunity to do it together and to have a much more lengthy debate with more Members involved. It is vitally important to the people of Canada and of the world.

May 1, 1984

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate this afternoon. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) for introducing the motion today as well as the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. All-mand) who spoke on the pressing problems of nuclear weapons and world conflicts that have occurred since World War II, and the intense building of nuclear arms. I will not repeat much of what has gone on, but I do want to put some of my concerns on the record.
I agree with the importance of this being a broader debate in Parliament. People throughout Canada should become more educated about the real danger of the nuclear holocaust and the events which could lead up to it. It would be devastating for the human race. I plan to circulate as widely as possible the speeches given in the House of Commons by all Members of Parliament who speak today, regardless of their political affiliation. It is a common cause and there is a common bond with regard to the issue we are debating.
I had the honour and the privilege of attending the Seventy-First Interparliamentary Conference in Geneva from April 2 to 7 of this year. We had a delegation in Geneva to discuss some issues that are pertinent to the debate today. Three topics were discussed at the interparliamentary conference: first, a panel on world population; second, an emergency resolution or supplementary item, as it was referred to, on the Iranian-Iraqi war, and, third, a panel on arms control and disarmament. I was proud to be part of the Canadian delegation on the latter panel, namely, that on arms control and disarmament.
The presentation by the Canadian delegation on that panel began by pointing out the peace initiatives of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the broad, if not unanimous acceptance of his peace initiatives by this Parliament and the Canadian people. It is worth putting on the record again today that, out of the findings of the peace initiatives that were started, and that must continue, there were ten principles that represented a common area of interest and agreement between East and West emerging from the wide-ranging discussions that were begun there. It is not only East and West but also the developing and developed countries that hold these concerns. The ten points are as follows: Both sides agree that a nuclear war cannot be won. Both sides agree that a nuclear war must never be fought. Both sides wish to be free of the risk of accidental or surprise attack. Both sides recognize the dangers inherent in destabilizing weapons. Both sides understand the need for improved techniques of crisis management. Both sides are conscious of the awesome consequences of being the first to use force against the other. Both sides have an interest in increasing security while reducing the cost. Both sides have an interest in avoiding the spread of nuclear weapons to other countries. Both sides have come to a guarded recognition of each other's legitimate security interests. Finally, both sides realize that their security strategies cannot be based on the assumed political or economic collapse of the other side. That would just not happen.
Further, the Canadian delegation at the interparliamentary conference in Geneva put forward the priorities officially supported by Canada. First, Canada will press for a comprehensive and multilateral nuclear test ban treaty. On this subject there is preparatory work in progress, and it has been going on for some time, so that Canadian parliamentarians and the Canadian people can contribute their share to what will be a difficult process of deliberations.
Second, Canada will be pressing for a more effective nonproliferation regime. I personally pointed out that although it is not currently part of Canada's official proposals, many parliamentarians and Canadian people are pressing for a policy of nuclear weapons-free zones. I applaud all those countries which forwarded this concept at the interparliamentary conference. There were some 100 countries in attendance at the conference, including all of the countries that presently have a nuclear weapons capability or have nuclear weapons within their arsenals.
Third, Canada will press for a convention to prohibit chemical weapons. Until such time as a convention can be put in place, we call upon countries of the world to confirm or re-confirm their adherence to the protocol agreement of 1925 banning the use of chemical weapons. This has come to the fore because of the situation arising from the Iranian-Iraqi war.
Fourth, officially Canada will press toward the objective of prohibiting all weapons from use in outer space. Certainly the development of weapons for use in outer space only further endangers the tinder box in which we now live. I believe we must maintain this last frontier for peaceful and mutually beneficial purposes.
In addition, on the official position of Canada we strongly put forward that we would support negotiations to limit and reduce nuclear arms. We would participate actively in negotiations to limit and reduce conventional forces. Further, we would seek step by step to achieve ultimately general and complete disarmament consistent with the legitimate security needs of states. This ties in very well with what the Hon. Member for Waterloo said about the need for an international police force to protect states that still fear aggression from other countries.
We all realize that the major stumbling blocks to arms control and disarmament agreements are the methods of monitoring or verification and the trust of others throughout the world. We must not let the problems that lie there be excuses for not being able to overcome those hurdles. Whether we consider ourselves East or West, developed or developing countries, we must look forward to the day with optimism when we will not have to explain to our children the atrocities of war or why weapons of mass destruction exist on the face of the earth.
May 1, 1984

We should always remember that not one of us owns any piece of this planet. Although we may have a deed to a piece of property, ultimately none of us own the planet. We have inherited this planet from past generations. We will let down future generations unless we find a way to pass it on, hopefully in a better state than when we found it. By allowing the escalation and threat of nuclear weapons to increase along with other weapons of mass destruction, we are not honouring that obligation to future generations.
I now want to turn to the resolution that was adopted at the Seventy-First Interparliamentary Conference in Geneva. The panel which dealt with the arms race, arms control and world disarmament passed this resolution unanimously. As I have already pointed out, all countries in the world which are governed by some form of Parliament, whether or not we in the free world agree with that form of Parliament, are represented at the inter-parliamentary union. This resolution was adopted unanimously.
I believe that the resolution covered the four points which were mentioned by the Hon. Member for Waterloo. I would like to look at a few of the highlights of that resolution today. Point No. 10 of the draft resolution reads as follows:
Calls upon Parliaments and Governments, especially those of the most heavily armed countries, to exert efforts for reducing the enormous expenditure entailed in accumulating arms for military purposes, as well as to channel the human and material potentials released by the reduction of military expenditure towards economic and social development, particularly for the benefit of the developing countries;
Point No. 12 of the resolution reads as follows:
Calls upon Parliaments and Governments to support the creation of nuclear-weapon-free zones in various parts of the world-particularly in areas of tension-wherever all the States of the region show interest and give their agreement;
I find this point to be of particular interest since I have put forward two private Member's Bills in an attempt to declare Canada a nuclear-weapons-free zone. In the last Parliament, I put forward Bill C-678, and in the first session of this Parliament, the session we are now in, I put forward Bill C-203. I must say that that Bill has received some support, just as the motion today is receiving some support from all sides of the House of Commons. I was gratified to find that this section of the motion was adopted by all member countries of the inter-parliamentary union.
Point 13(a) of the resolution to which I have referred reads as follows:
To initiate parliamentary debates on disarmament problems, to launch appeals and issue statements in favour of the cessation of the arms build-up, to adopt measures freezing and reducing-military expenditure, to support the prohibition of foreign bases and troops on the territory of other States and the disbanding of military blocs;
Point No. 13(b) reads as follows:
To intensify parliamentary contacts on the regional and sub-regional levels on such problems as the strengthening of confidence and security, the creation of areas of co-operation, understanding and neighbourliness, without nuclear weapons;
Disarmament
I believe that the Members who have risen in the House today and the Members who will rise after me have no problem agreeing with that point. I encourage the parliamentarians who are here today and the Canadian people who have followed and will be following this debate to educate our friends and neighbours to promote international peace and arms control and certainly to promote the reduction and elimination of nuclear weapons so that all of mankind can live in a better world.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REDUCING NUCLEAR WEAPONS AND RESUMING DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because other members wish to speak in this debate, I will keep my remarks quite brief. However, I wish to note that this debate has two distinguishing characteristics. First, there is representation in support of the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) from all sides of the House. This is a non-partisan debate and indeed it is a high level debate. I believe that the issues which have been put forward have been approached from a level of deep political concern in a way that lifts us above partisan debate.
The second characteristic of this debate is the unique nature of the motion before us which is being introduced internationally in many Parliaments throughout the world. Just as we here in Canada are speaking in this hour that is available to us, so too there are parliamentarians in other nations who are addressing in their own Chambers the very same questions. To me, this represents a very significant gain in the international understanding of our common concerns and the understanding of the common ground on which we all stand as we seek collective security with economic development for all, the only sane course of action for a world which has become not only international but truly interdependent. We do live in a global community and it is those of us who are specifically charged as elected politicians in national legislatures who must rise above the domestic concerns which are always real and pressing and put into place a system that will ensure true security with economic development in the world.
I wish to take a moment to note that one of the leaders of the United Nations, Mr. Brad Morse, the administrator of the United Nations Development Program, spoke at one of the first forums that was held at the United Nations by Parliamentarians for World Order, the organization which has sponsored the very motion we are debating. Mr. Morse was a distinguished Republican Congressman in the United States Congress before moving on to his post at the United Nations. I would like to read the words of Mr. Morse to indicate to my colleagues what today's debate is all about. Mr. Morse said:
We have to make a great and noble leap in our thinking about profound issues of public policy, from parish to planet; from nation to United Nations; from abject poverty for most of our human family to progress in equity and well-being for all; from the tragic absurdity of armaments to the sanity of peace that can ennoble and enrich all of us.
The most recent forum held by Parliamentarians for World Order at the United Nations last November was a forum which was conducted under the title "Global Militarization versus Economic Development". It was a forum which tried to relate these two principal concerns in life today, development

May 1, 1984
Disarmament
and disarmament. It was a forum which tried to show that the two characteristics of our world today are militarization and deprivation and one which tried to show that the East-West conflict has North-South dimensions as well. These are the global concerns that this organization has tried to put forward.
At that forum, the keynote speaker was the distinguished Secretary-General of the Commonwealth, Mr. Shridath Ram-phal, a man who is well known in our country. To be frank about it, Sir, he gave the forum a rather gloomy prognosis of the state of the world today. I would like to read to the House a few of the words with which Mr. Ramphal left us, because they are words worth pondering. He said:
We are losing the ethic of peaceful settlement. Resort to force is becoming less disreputable. In fact, the gravest contradiction of all may arise if democracy begins to stand in the way of internationalism as the notion takes root that there are votes in war. We allow the machinery of peacemaking to rust away. It it any wonder that militarism is ascendant?
That, unfortunately, is a characteristic of the world in which we live today. My colleagues have already pointed out the enormous amounts of money that are being spent on the arms race literally at the cost of the poor of the world.
Mr. Ramphal went on to make another point, and I would like to conclude my remarks on this note. He said:
Whatever the lunacies of the rich, why do poor countries persist in adding to their military budgets? ... In an international climate dominated by militarism, some Third World leaders have sadly allowed themselves to regard modern weapons systems almost as symbols of progress or as necessary props for political power... What is needed is a new global ethos that rejects the military culture.
That indeed is the challenge that we as parliamentarians face when trying to grapple with larger responsibilities.
I would like to conclude by saying that last week I visited Peru. To see an example of what a combination of militarism and deprivation does to a people, one would only have to look at the people of that country. In that country, 45 per cent of the budget is spent on military armaments, the army and all the accoutrements that go with modern warfare. All of that is at the expense of the greatest deprivation that I have seen in my many years of travelling through Third World countries. It was brought home to me very forcefully.
In the nuclear arms race the major nations of the world- the five permanent member nations of the Security Council which have weapons and, in particular, the two superpowers that have 95 per cent of all the nuclear weapons in the world- are continuing to build a vertical mountain of nuclear weaponry, while other nations of the world are extending a horizontal network of conventional arms in ways that are horrendous to contemplate in terms of their economies and also are manifesting a militaristic culture. I believe we have to consider seriously how to get rid of it.
Even if the world could eliminate all nuclear weapons, which it seems is a political impossibility, the world from then on would have to live with the knowledge of how to construct nuclear weapons. I put this question to the distinguished Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) and I ask him to consider it. I put this question to him very seriously and I know
he may have an opportunity to respond tonight. How is it possible, as a new political challenge, to make knowledge-as distinct from actual possession-the actual deterrence? This course of action has been labelled by Jonathan Schell among others as "existential deterrence". This would entail the abolition of nuclear arms in progressive steps, starting with a reciprocal no-first-use pledge.
The threat of deterrence would ultimately consist of the ability of one side to construct nuclear devices once it was known that the other side was doing so. The critical time factor of split-second death would be removed. On the basis of my experience as a politician, I recognize that the chances of moving into such a mode are quite remote without a tremendous political push forward. I believe that Canada has a real role to play in making a contribution to the verification systems in the world that need to be developed both in conventional arms, as we are doing in the contributions that the Canadian Government has made so far to the Stockholm Conference, and in the verification techniques that still have to be developed for outer space weapons in order to stop that escalation of nuclear technology beyond the point where it is today.
I make a very fervent appeal to my colleagues in this House to take very seriously the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Waterloo, because it has opened up the very high level, non-partisan way in which we are speaking on behalf of humanity. Indeed, we are speaking about the survival of my children as well as the children of every Member of this House of Commons and their grandchildren. That is our responsibility. I believe that Parliamentarians for World Order have helped to lift up our thinking, and now as politicians we will have to follow it through.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I support this motion very strongly, but I support it as a second step rather than a first step. I would like to give an idea of where I think we should go first. This, I think, is tremendously important. I think many Hon. Members have seen the cartoon about the two men knee-deep in gasoline. One of them has seven matches and the other has ten matches. The matches represent nuclear weapons. Both of them are arguing about who has more matches and whether one has bigger matches than the other. It seems to me that the argument of how many nuclear weapons we have in this particular proposal is part of the solution to that argument. I have become convinced that we are working from the wrong place to start with. Maybe we should be draining the gasoline from the tanks, because we are not getting anywhere by just making these proposals.
I was very pleased when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke on February 9 as a result of long discussions he had with leaders of many, many countries around the world, including the major NATO countries, the Warsaw Pact countries, the five nuclear powers, and, in particular, the two superpowers. He came to a series of conclusions. I think that these conclusions may be the very basis for the beginning of the kind of negotiations that would bring us to a freeze. I would like to mention these quickly. The Prime Minister said that there is
May 1, 1984

among all of these nations, including the superpowers: agreement that a nuclear war cannot be won; agreement that a nuclear war must never be fought; a wish to be free of accidental war or of surprise attack; recognition of the dangers of destabilizing weapons; the need for improved techniques of crisis management; recognition of the consequences of the first use of force; an interest in increasing security and reducing costs; prevention of horizontal proliferation; recognition of each other's legitimate security interests; and, finally, recognition that their security cannot be based on the political or economic collapse of the other side.
It seems to me that if we start with this-and I met with a group in the United States just recently who were talking about a common ground-it would provide the common ground. I hope the Prime Minister, when he leaves here, will carry on with the idea that these particular points could be a basis for a group of countries which would be involved in some kind of third party action to bring the two superpowers and the other nuclear powers to recognize that we must come to the point of freeze. I believe the gasoline must be drained from the tank before there can be agreement on a freeze.
Admiral Eugene Carroll said the other night that he felt a nuclear war was probable by about 1992. We must move to do the two things I am suggesting.

subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-PROCUREMENT OF ARMOUR-PLATED AUTOMOBILES. (B) REPORTED DEFICIENCIES IN VEHICLES
SUPPLY AND SERVICES-PROCUREMENT OF ARMOUR-PLATED AUTOMOBILES. (B) REPORTED DEFICIENCIES IN VEHICLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the questions I have asked in the House, and on the Order Paper, regarding the purchase of special vehicles to protect diplomats and our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), are really designed to bring to the attention of the Government some rather startling deficiencies and, may I say, inefficiencies.
For example, what is the role of Mr. John Morgan, reportedly retired from the American secret service? Who recommended him as an expert in this area for our purposes in Canada? There is also the bidding process itself, and interdepartmental squabbling and reported paranoia between the RCMP, the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Supply and Services, and officious people involved in these Departments such as Superintendent Muir of the RCMP, Mr. Steve MacEachern from the Department of Supply and Services, and Mr. Barry Weaymouth from the Department of External Affairs who recently went off on another trip to Miami.
I am, of course, concerned to see that the mechanical deficiencies with the summit seven cars are remedied, particularly the problems with the glass. I would like to know if Hesse Eisenhardt, who supplied these cars will again be able to escape any guarantee provisions. What were the results of the

May 1, 1984
Adjournment Debate
legal opinions with respect to the glass deficiencies in these cars? Was there any reason why the Canadian Government decided not to sue the company for these deficiencies? Taxpayers are entitled to know these things even if some egos in various departments are bruised.
What is the process which allows the Department of External Affairs to take the risk with our diplomats in the field? Also, I wonder if the Minister will produce the external affairs report of the internal audit of emergency buys for bulletproof vehicles?
With regard to the Prime Minister's new limousine, which he does not like because the windows do not open, I assume Mr. Morgan had some role in purchasing this car. Is the price we paid for the Prime Minister's vehicule the same, allowing for currency differences, as that paid for a similar vehicle for the President of the U.S.? What role did Superintendent Muir and Sergeant Banks of the RCMP play in this matter? Were specifications drafted by Sergeant Banks, changed by Superintendent Muir, and, if so, was there any good reason for it?
With respect to the vehicles known as "Popemobiles" which are being purchased-I understand there are three Oldsmo-biles-John Morgan, apparently is involved, but where does this leave Sergeant Banks who was offered to the Department of External Affairs as an expert? Also, why is John Morgan signing his name as an RCMP member, as he did on February 22 when he entered the protective materials plant in Miami? Also, was this contract a predetermined contract, as with respect to the Prime Minister's limousine, but with all the fanfare of a legitimate bid?
I am very skeptical that the taxpayers of Canada are getting value for their money. I am skeptical about the legitimacy of the bidding process and I am very suspicious of what I consider to be the incompetence and the in-fighting I detected in the Departments concerned.
I would also like to know if there is an approximate $30,000 differential per vehicle in some instances between the Hesse Eisenhardt bid and that of another supplier, and, if so, how do you explain this attitude towards the bidding process? Why do so many vehicles appear to be predestined to be bought from the Hesse Eisenhardt Company, particularly when there are reports that this company may be the subject of yet another change in ownership?
I will have other questions, Mr. Speaker. I would like to have some sign that the Government recognizes that there is a problem, that it is prepared to be honest in assessing the causes, and is taking the actions required to remedy the situation.

subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-PROCUREMENT OF ARMOUR-PLATED AUTOMOBILES. (B) REPORTED DEFICIENCIES IN VEHICLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the question put by the Member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) on April 12 of this year. Following an exhaustive study of possible sources of supply, a contract for a 1983
model Cadillac Fleetwood limousine was given to Hesse Eisenhardt in August 1983.
Both Canadian and American companies appeared on the list of prospective suppliers of the Department of Supply and Services. However, none of the domestic companies was able to supply a vehicle with the type of armour-plating desired. The RCMP then consulted the U.S. Secret Service, which replied that the only American company capable of supplying an armoured vehicle meeting the security standards for the President of the United States was Hesse Eisenhardt. Consequently, the RCMP asked the Department of Supply and Services to negotiate a contract with Hesse Eisenhardt, for supplying the limousine.
As far as the Summit meeting is concerned, it is correct that seven cars, made by Chevrolet and provided with armour-plating by Hesse Eisenhardt, were purchased for that occasion. As far as I know, there was never any mention of deficiencies in the armour-plating of these vehicles. However, there may have been complaints about certain mechanical deficiencies. In fact, no manufacturing defects could be found in any of the armoured vehicles acquired on behalf of the Department of External Affairs. I must point out, however, that further questions on the subject would have to be answered by the Department of External Affairs rather than the Department of Supply and Services.
As for the purchase of vehicles required for the Pope's visit in September 1984, to which the Hon. Member for Pembina seemed to be referring, the RCMP has recommended calling for tenders. Furthermore, a number of companies have asked the Department of Supply and Services to let them bid on the contract. It was therefore decided to assess the capabilities of prospective suppliers by sending each one a call for tender. Eleven companies, both Canadian and American, received an invitation to bid, and each company's capabilities have been thoroughly examined. The overriding criterion for selecting a supplier was the availability of the type of steel required for armour-plating. Although Protective Materials International Inc. of Miami Lakes, Florida, made a lower bid, it was felt that since the company did not have the required steel in stock, it would not be able to get it from the manufacturer in time for the delivery deadline.
In view of the urgent nature of the order, it was decided to give the contract to Hesse Eisenhardt. In fact, this company was the only one to have enough of the right kind of steel in stock and the expertise required to do the armour-plating within the established time frame. Consequently, a contract for Can. $358,725 was given Hess and Eisenhardt on March 6, 1984.

subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT-LINGAN-PHELEN COAL MINE PROJECT IN NOVA SCOTIA. (B) LACK OF EMPLOYMENT
REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT-LINGAN-PHELEN COAL MINE PROJECT IN NOVA SCOTIA. (B) LACK OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 11, 1984 I raised a question in the House with the Minister responsible for regional and industrial expansion (Mr. Lumley). The question arose from the tragic fire at Devco's No. 26 colliery in Cape Breton.
As the Minister knows, 1,400 people are out of work because of the fire. The Leader of the New Democratic Party in Nova Scotia sent a telegram to the Minister calling on the Government to speed up development of the coal mine, a move which would provide jobs and spare these people severe economic hardship. I am advised that to this date nothing has changed in that regard. The situation is the same as it was two and one-half weeks ago. They need assistance to get another mine going. There are 1,400 miners out of work. The unemployment rate is 30 per cent to 40 per cent. There was a wire sent which reads as follows:
Due to the serious fire and sealing off of No. 26 colliery Glace Bay and loss of over twelve hundred jobs District 26 United Mine Workers of America executive and membership request you press for the immediate opening of Lingan-Phelen mine and three new mines from one slope at former Number 20 colliery Glace Bay to alleviate any further unemployment in this area.
In his answer to me the Minister indicated that:
My officials have been working since Friday with the Devco officials to bring this information to my attention. It is hoped that we can make a decision with respect to the new mine as soon as possible.
That is not good enough. The problem is that there are contracts of sale involved here. We know that the American government is aggressively moving toward an attempt to get contracts with Korean and Japanese markets. Unless there are very serious moves made soon we would lose these markets and these jobs could be gone forever.
Also, with regard to a wire we received concerning a telegram which was addressed to the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts), I would hope that the Parliamentary Secretary would relay this message to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It states:
The United Mine Workers of America District Executive Board is requesting Minister of Employment and Immigration for the immediate lifting of the waiting period for men from the 26th colliery who because of the disaster of the fire will have to wait additional time to qualify for UIC.
Again, because of the inaction of the Government, these workers are unable to collect their unemployment benefits. In our opinion, they are unnecessarily being laid off. There are programs put forward for the opening up of other areas or slopes. They have now sealed off the fire but the situation is exactly the same. These workers need help and they need it now.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-UNEMPLOYMENT IN ATLANTIC CANADA-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S ADVICE. (B) PLIGHT OF JOBLESS
LABOUR CONDITIONS-UNEMPLOYMENT IN ATLANTIC CANADA-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S ADVICE. (B) PLIGHT OF JOBLESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 12 I raised the matter of the desperate situation in which the Atlantic provinces find themselves, and have found themselves over the past number of months with respect to the unemployment that exists there. I specifically referred to the construction trades in and around the Saint John region, Moncton, Bathurst and Campbellton. Quite frankly, we find it intolerable.
I mentioned in the House before that the norm in the construction trades seems to be in the vicinity of 75 per cent to 83 per cent unemployment, which basically covers the entire construction trade segment. The frustration of these people is that there does not seem to be any sort of a response from the Government to the plight in which they find themselves.
For instance, in the Saint John region a new hotel complex recently opened up with a mere handful of jobs in relation to the number of unemployed in that region. For somewhere in the vicinity of say 150 to 200 jobs there was a lineup of over 1,500 people who were making job applications. Some people stood literally all night in that line-up so they would be the first to be considered for a job. The management of the hotel complex had to bring in a team of people to process the applicants who were lined up for those jobs.

May 1, 1984
Adjournment Debate
In the shipyard in Saint John we find a union with approximately 1,100 to 1,200 members, with nine people as of yesterday working in that yard. Imagine nine people out of a complement of 1,100 to 1,200 workers in one of the most modern shipyards in the country, probably in North America. This Government has spent a lot of money developing that yard, but it has not done a single thing to pump any sort of meaningful work into that yard that would create jobs for more than a handful of people. That is the frustration, Mr. Speaker.
We now find that the City of Moncton has the highest unemployment of any city across this nation. That is totally unacceptable. The City of Moncton is supposed to be the hub of the Maritimes. It is supposed to be the rail centre for the CNR with its repair depots. But what do we hear, Sir? We have heard consistently over the last number of months, and the past couple of years, of lay-off after lay-off after lay-off in a Crown corporation that is directly controlled by this Government. This Government should be addressing itself to finding meaningful ways to increasing employment in that Crown corporation in Moncton which so desperately needs jobs instead of lay-offs.
We have been attempting for months and months to encourage this Government to increase grain shipments through the Port of Saint John. We are not asking for many, but one or two additional shipments during the season would make a tremendous difference to the amount of work created in that port. The Port of Saint John is one of the finest facilities in North America. It is one of those rare ports with the capacity, the capability and the work force to handle most any circumstance of shipping that we could possibly conceive of or require. This Government cannot come to grips or cope with the desperate situation that exists in the Port of Saint John, even by increasing the number of grain shipments by an additional one or two, which is all we were asking.
Speaking of the Port of Saint John, we could easily consider in a meaningful way the creation of a free trade zone. It has an ideal geographical location. The Maritime region of New Brunswick is next to the great market of New England with its 48 million people, practically twice the population of Canada. Imagine the benefit to the Maritime region, to the Port of Saint John and to that entire area if the Port of Saint John were declared a free trade zone. What about the literally billions of dollars in additional revenues that could be generated over a short period of time, creating jobs in a region that is starved economically for the maintenance of its current job level?
There are many things to which this Government could address itself to alleviate the difficulties which the Atlantic and Maritime region is facing. Instead, this Government seems to be contented with the attitude of, "send down a few paltry dollars from time to time through a new Government job creation program which will dry up in a few months, only to keep the soup kitchens rolling. It is difficult for most people in the country to realize that soup kitchens are on the increase.
Not since the great depression have we seen anything like we are currently experiencing. It is a sad fact of life, but, due to the apathy of government, the number of soup lines is on the increase.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Dubois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-UNEMPLOYMENT IN ATLANTIC CANADA-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S ADVICE. (B) PLIGHT OF JOBLESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first point out that, according to the latest unemployment data as compiled by economic region and published by Statistics Canada-they are for the week ending March 17-it is not in Moncton that the unemployment rate is the highest. With 18.6 per cent unemployment, this city ranks twelfth.
While unemployment is admittedly a serious problem in New Brunswick and indeed elsewhere, it is heartening to note that unemployment in that province did fall from 15 per cent in December 1983 to 14.7 per cent in March 1984. For Canada as a whole, during the same period, unemployment has increased by .3 per cent. All the signs show that the economy of New Brunswick, which is getting close to the pre-recession level, should continue to improve this year. According to the Conference Board reports, the mining, manufacturing and construction sectors should also show substantial growth. In fact, the housing construction, pulp and paper, lumber production and retail industries already show a marked increase compared with last year's performance. Opportunities are therefore improving for New Brunswick workers.
The Minister has already mentioned the frigate program. The $3.9 million contract granted to the Saint John Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Co. Ltd. will certainly prove to be beneficial to the economy of the Saint John area. Included in the construction projects are the Maritime Forestry Complex in Fredericton at a cost of $45 million, the restoration plans for downtown Moncton at a cost of $41 million and the development of the Sussex potash mines.
Unemployment and conditions prevailing in the building sector and the various industries of Atlantic Canada are matters of ongoing concern to us. However, in view of the improvement in the economic picture and the new projects now underway such as the frigate program, the Government is convinced that still more jobs will be created.
I therefore urge the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) to promote the projects and programs developed by the Canadian Government; I am sure he is pleased with them and will be glad to tell all and sundry that Saint John Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Co. Ltd. in New Brunswick have been awarded a $3.9 million contract and that the $42 million Fredericton Maritime Forestry Complex and the $41 million improvement program in downtown Moncton are the workings of the Liberal Government led by Mr. Trudeau. These programs are aimed at improving the situation in Atlantic Canada and more especially in New Brunswick. All the work
May 1, 1984

done under the job creation programs such as the temporary job creation programs slashed by the Conservative Government in 1979 and brought back by the Liberal Government will result in an improved situation in New Brunswick.
